I have played and enjoyed counterstrike for over 10 years. This was once my favorite game and I enjoyed collecting skins and watching all the majors. I was never very good (usually high silver or low gold) but I always had fun as a casual player and looked forward to relaxing playing counterstrike with friends after work. Today I played a competitive match on Office, I was doing ok but not great and we were about halfway through the match when I saw a red message on the screen that said the match was cancelled due to VAC detecting irregular gameplay. I was so happy and excited to finally see an anti cheat in action for counterstrike, but when I got back to my solo lobby I saw i had a 20 hour global cooldown. The only details it gave was VAC detected irregular gameplay and when I go to my steam account, the listed reason for the VAC cooldown is: "Unexpected Error". I am extremely disappointed, frustrated, and sad at valve for letting this happen. The only thing worse than having no anticheat or a bad anticheat, is an ai based anticheat that gives out false bans or cooldowns. I have submitted a ticket already but I doubt I will ever hear back from a real person. I have accumulated a significant inventory over the years I have been playing and collecting skins but now I am terrified to ever play again after my 20 hour cooldown expires. After looking into this there are several well known players and streamers who have recently experienced this issue too within the last few months. I feel really let down to have to give up my favorite game with no choice but I won't play a game giving false cooldowns when I have never cheated in any way. I don't want to risk my inventory or my steam account with so many memories either. If you have an inventory worth any meaningful amount or your steam account has any meaning to you, do not risk playing counterstrike in its current state. Wait for the VAC live system to get to a functional state. This used to be my favorite game, now I just feel betrayed after pouring so much time and money into it. 0 10, find a different game to play.

This game saved my life. I am 28. My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and adopted our son together. They are now both 4 years old. When we were going through our separation, I found myself lost and miserable. I was self destructive. I got so mad one day from everything spiraling out of my control that I punched some concrete in a moment of overwhelming emotion. That caused me to break my 5th metacarpal in my right hand... my working hand... my games hand.. the hand that I held and carried my children to bed with.. The hand I desperately needed to make sure I could continue to provide. After learning of the severity of my self-inflicted damage, I was borderline suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man with no history of depression or anxiety. I have never had fits of rage, or been one to break down and cry, but I was in a low spot that just really buried me from being able to see the light on the other side. Having nothing better to do, I searched for a game I could play, ONE HANDED while I recovered. I somehow stumbled upon this game and read some of the reviews. I decided that it had to be worth a shot... I must admit, I didn't beat the game, or play nearly as long as some of you. In fact, I may have only played this game a day or two.. With that being said, after doing so, I had a new found joy and hope for life. I was able to put behind me the pain and suffering that had been cast over me. I was able to experience other peoples joy and happiness. I was able to see the fruits of my "labor". I relaxed for 5 minutes to this music long enough to realize that I was going to be okay. After coming to that realization, I turned the game off, and I went back to work. It hurt my hand like hell but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so damn sorry for myself, and I became the father I needed to be in that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving as. Today, I am close friend with my kids mother. We don't fight, or argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents, and friends. I now have 3 kids. My third child is, wait for it, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my own separation, and we just stumbled in to each others life unexpectedly. We have been in a relationship for a year now, and are very happy together. Moral of the story, you never know what life holds in store for you, and if I would have given up when all the odds were stacked against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that. Thank you

Recommended What light through yonder monitor breaks? It is the flashbang, and Counter-Strike 2 is the sun. Good gentles all, lend me thine ears, for I must speak of a marvel wrought not by alchemists nor kings, but by the cunning artificers of Valve. Verily, I did enter this game but seeking brief diversion, and lo, three hundred hours vanished as swiftly as a thief in the night. Upon these digital fields do warriors gather, armed with rifles, pistols, and the confidence of men who have watched one too many tutorials. Here are forged friendships stronger than steel and rivalries bitter enough to sour the finest wine in Christendom. Never have I witnessed such passion as when five souls unite in pursuit of victory, nor such tragedy as when one fellow insisteth upon buying a Negev every round. The gunplay? Exquisite. Each shot ringeth with purpose, each duel becometh a test of wit, nerve, and mechanical prowess. To land a perfect headshot is to feel as Caesar crossing the Rubicon; to whiff an entire magazine at point-blank range is to experience Hamlet's despair firsthand. And what of the smokes? Ah, the smokes! They billow and twist like ghosts upon a moonlit heath, changing the very shape of battle itself. Many a time have I cast one forth with the confidence of a seasoned general, only to discover I had blinded mine own companions and doomed us all. Such is the nature of genius. The maps stand as great stages upon which this endless drama unfolds. Dust II, ancient and eternal, remaineth the theatre where heroes rise and fools rush through mid with an AWP. Mirage breedeth schemes and stratagems most devious. Inferno turneth every banana into a corridor of fear and flaming death. Yet no review would be complete without mention of the creatures who inhabit these lands. Some are noble knights who offer wisdom and encouragement. Others possess vocabularies composed entirely of insults and microphone static. Together they form a tapestry most magnificent, a living portrait of humanity in all its glory and madness. There are moments of triumph so sweet that one feeleth invincible. There are defeats so crushing that one stareth silently at the wall and reconsidereth every life choice that led to queuing for "just one more match." And yet, despite heartbreak, despite despair, despite the teammate who disconnecteth whilst holding the bomb, I always return. For Counter-Strike 2 is not merely a game. It is a comedy, a tragedy, a history, and at times a psychological experiment. It hath brought me joy, suffering, exhilaration, confusion, and an unhealthy knowledge of smoke lineups. Would I recommend it? A thousand times yes. Though all the world be but a stage, Counter-Strike 2 is the finest one upon which I have ever missed an easy shot. Hours played: Far too many. Hours regretted: None.

Rust Review, 5,000 Hours Later Rust is a survival game where you start naked on a beach with a rock, a torch, and a dream. That dream usually lasts about 47 seconds before someone with an AK, night vision, and serious personal issues turns you into a loot bag. I have spent 5,000 hours playing Rust. In that time, I have built bases, farmed stone, crafted weapons, made alliances, been betrayed, been raided, lost everything, rebuilt, got raided again, and somehow convinced myself that this time will be different. It never is. Rust is basically an abusive relationship with extra door codes. You spend hours building the perfect base, carefully honeycombing it, adding traps, sorting boxes, upgrading walls, feeling like a genius. Then you log in the next day and find a hole where your house used to be and a sign outside saying thanks for the loot . And yet, I keep coming back. I die a lot. I build a lot. I get raided a lot. I still have no idea how some 12-year-old with a bow has better aim than a trained sniper. After 5,000 hours, I can confidently say I have not won Rust. I am not even sure Rust can be won. Rust is pain, paranoia, farming, betrayal, and waking up at 3am to check if your base still exists. 10 10, would lose everything again.

Executive Summary Counter-Strike 2 (CS2) was marketed as a revolutionary leap forward for tactical shooters, built on the Source 2 engine. In reality, it has functioned as a forced, incomplete replacement for Counter-Strike: Global Offensive (CS:GO). By deleting a polished, decade-refined esport and replacing it with a fundamentally flawed product, Valve has downgraded the core gameplay experience, ruined competitive integrity, and alienated its most dedicated player base. 1. Technical Performance The "Sub-Tick" Illusion The foundation of any competitive tactical shooter is consistency and visual clarity. CS2 fails catastrophically here. The Sub-Tick Failure: Valve replaced traditional 128-tick servers with a proprietary "sub-tick" architecture. While advertised as calculating actions between ticks, the real-world result is severe desynchronization. Players routinely experience dying behind solid walls, delayed kill registration, and rubber-banding. What you see on your screen rarely aligns with what the server decides happened. Performance Degradation: The Source 2 engine introduced heavy particle effects (volumetric smoke, molotov fire) that cause massive frame-rate drops, even on high-end hardware. Micro-stutters and 1 low FPS drops make smooth tracking impossible, destroying the fluid movement that CS was famous for. The "Michael Jackson" and Animation Bugs: Hitboxes regularly desynchronize from character models, particularly during jumping, crouching, or rapid peeking, turning precise aiming into a lottery. 2. Total Collapse of Anti-Cheat and Competitive Integrity Competitive matchmaking is entirely unplayable at high levels due to a total lack of effective oversight. The Non-Existent Anti-Cheat: Valve s automated anti-cheat systems (VAC VACnet) are a laughingstock compared to intrusive kernel-level competitors. Rage-hackers (spin-bots, wallhacks, instant headshots through doors) run rampant in the Premier matchmaking mode without consequence. The Third-Party Necessity: The fact that players are forced to download third-party software (like Faceit) just to experience a match free of blatant cheaters is a definitive admission that Valve s core product is broken. Rank Inflation and Matchmaking Chaos: Premier rating points are deeply flawed, routinely matching solo-queue players against coordinated five-stack teams, resulting in stomps rather than competitive games. 3. Disastrous Casual Community Support Valve didn't just release a bad game; they actively stripped away content that players loved for years. Stolen Content: CS2 launched by deleting half of CS:GO's game modes. Missing maps, the removal of the iconic Arms Race (for months), Retakes, and Danger Zone stripped the game of its variety. Murdering the Community Server Browser: The community server browser the literal lifeblood that birthed Counter-Strike through custom maps, surf, jailbreak, and zombie modes is clunky, broken, and practically buried. By suffocating the community modding scene, Valve turned a diverse gaming ecosystem into a sterile storefront. 4. Prioritizing Gambling Content Over Gameplay The development cycle of CS2 heavily implies where Valve s actual priorities lie. Case Simulator with a Side of Shooter: Weapon finishes, knife skins, and cases function perfectly. While netcode, sub-tick fixes, and anti-cheat updates are delayed or ineffective, the steam market and case-opening mechanics remain flawless. The game operates more as a decentralized virtual casino than a competitive tactical esport. Conclusion: The Final Verdict Score: 3 10 Counter-Strike 2 is a massive step backward. Valve took a masterpiece of competitive balance (CS:GO), deleted it from existence so players couldn't go back, and forced an unpolished, cheater-infested, sub-tick experiment onto the community. It is a game that does not respect its players' time, competitive drive, or PC hardware. Until Valve introduces a functional anti-cheat and fixes the desynced netcode, CS2 is an embarrassing regression that is not worth your time.

Rust is genuinely one of the greatest survival games ever made, and I do not say that lightly. This game is pure chaos, pure pain, pure comedy, and pure addiction all wrapped into one brutal masterpiece. There is no other game that can make you feel like an unstoppable warlord one minute and a homeless caveman begging for mercy the next. Rust is not just a game you play. Rust is a full psychological experience. The best thing about Rust is that nothing is ever guaranteed. You can spawn on the beach with nothing but a rock and a torch, get chased by a naked man screaming into his mic, somehow survive, farm enough materials to build a starter base, and then two hours later you are deep in a snow biome fighting full metal AK players over an airdrop. Every single wipe feels like a completely different story. Some wipes you snowball instantly. Some wipes you get doorcamped by the most unemployed human beings on Earth. Some wipes you become the villain. Some wipes the server makes you the victim. That is what makes it so good. The progression in Rust is insanely satisfying. Going from a stone hatchet and bow to furnaces, guns, explosives, electricity, turrets, compounds, and raids feels better than almost any progression system in gaming. Every item matters because you worked for it. Every gun feels valuable because you either farmed for it, crafted it, stole it, or risked everything to bring it home. Getting your first SAR, Thompson, or AK of the wipe feels like winning the lottery. Getting back to base with a full inventory of farm while hearing footsteps nearby is more intense than most horror games. The PvP is another reason Rust is so legendary. The fights are messy, stressful, and rewarding. Positioning matters. Aim matters. Game sense matters. Confidence matters. Even with all the chaos, there is a real skill gap. You can tell when someone knows how to move, when to peek, when to fall back, when to bait, when to push, and when to just run for their life. Every fight feels personal because there is actual risk. You are not just losing a round. You are losing the kit you farmed, crafted, or stole. That makes every kill feel amazing and every death feel like a crime against humanity. Base building is honestly one of the most underrated parts of the game. Rust lets you be creative in a way most survival games do not. You can make a tiny 2x1 shack, a bunker base, a cave base, a clan compound, a trap base, a roleplayer mansion, or the most disgusting honeycombed fortress known to man. There is so much depth in building that it almost feels like its own separate game. Learning how to protect loot, place doors correctly, hide TC, design peaks, add external TCs, set up turrets, and make your base annoying to raid is genuinely fun. Nothing feels better than logging on and seeing your base survived the night. The social side of Rust is what makes it completely unmatched. This game has some of the funniest, weirdest, most toxic, and most memorable interactions in gaming. You will meet random nakeds who become allies for the whole wipe. You will meet neighbors who act friendly and then betray you the second they get a chance. You will meet clans that treat a video game wipe like a military operation. You will hear the most unhinged voice chat imaginable. Rust creates stories naturally. You do not need scripted missions because the players are the content. Raiding is one of the most adrenaline-filled things in any game. The moment you start throwing satchels, rockets, or C4, everything changes. You hear counters coming. You hear doors opening. You wonder if the base owner is online. You wonder if you brought enough boom. You wonder if the loot is going to be insane or if you just wasted hours raiding a base full of pumpkins and waterpipes. The uncertainty is what makes it so good. A successful raid can change your entire wipe. A failed raid can ruin your night. That risk is exactly why it is exciting. Rust also keeps getting better because the game is constantly evolving. The map, monuments, weapons, vehicles, events, boats, trains, oil rigs, labs, cargo, helicopters, electricity, farming, industrial systems, and so many other features give players endless ways to play. You can be a PvPer, farmer, builder, electrician, fisherman, roleplayer, trap base goblin, ocean rat, monument runner, clan leader, solo grub, or just a menace to society. The game gives you tools and lets you decide what kind of creature you want to become. And honestly, Rust looks and feels way better than people give it credit for. The environments can be beautiful, especially during sunrise or sunset. Snow biomes, forests, deserts, beaches, and monuments all have their own vibe. Then five seconds later someone is shooting at you from a bush and the beauty turns into panic. That contrast is perfect. Rust can be peaceful when you are farming wood at night with the sound of the ocean nearby, and then instantly turn into a warzone because a naked with an eoka decided your existence was offensive. Is Rust frustrating? Absolutely. Is it toxic? Definitely. Will you lose hours of progress to the dumbest thing imaginable? Yes. Will you rage? Yes. Will you say you are done with the game forever and then load it back up the next day? Also yes. But that is exactly what makes Rust special. The highs are so high because the lows are brutal. The game does not hold your hand, and that is why every win feels earned. Rust is not for everyone, but for the people who understand it, there is nothing else like it. It is one of the only games where every wipe feels like a story you actually lived through. You remember the base you built, the neighbors you hated, the raid you barely won, the kit you lost, the snowball that changed everything, and the random guy who betrayed you after you gave him a bag. No other game creates memories like Rust. Overall, Rust is a masterpiece of survival, PvP, betrayal, creativity, and pure chaos. It is painful, hilarious, stressful, rewarding, and insanely addictive. It is the kind of game that can ruin your mood and still make you call it peak gaming. Rust is not just good. Rust is legendary.

These are Hellraiser, Stranger things chapter1 (which was brought back due to chapter 2) and Halloween. Not Recommended (and honestly, I should ve known better) 200 hours played. That s not a flex. That s a warning sign. You don t play this game anymore you maintain it like a second job you never applied for. You spawn naked on a beach with a rock and a torch. Sounds like a survival game, right? Wrong. It s a punishment loop disguised as progression. Within minutes you re reminded what the game actually is: Target practice for players with thousands of hours Free loot delivery service Background noise for someone screaming in voice chat There s no learning curve. Just a cliff. You think you re progressing, grinding resources, building something meaningful. In reality, you re just stockpiling items for the next guy who logs in while you re asleep. The building system is good technically. But what s the point of a good system when everything you build is temporary by design? You don t own anything in this game. You re just borrowing it until someone else takes it. The community gets described as chaotic or funny, but let s be honest: It s wildly inconsistent at best and straight-up unbearable at worst. For every genuinely funny interaction, you get ten that make you question why voice chat exists. And the time sink? Just one more run turns into hours of repetitive farming with zero payoff. Not because you made a mistake just because someone else had more time than you. At some point it stops being engaging and starts being exhausting. Pros: It hooks you (not in a good way) Solid mechanics wasted on a punishing loop Unpredictability mostly negative Cons: Progress means nothing longterm Encourages unhealthy play habits Community can be outright miserable Constant loss with no real payoff Playtime: Too much to justify Fun: Questionable Respect for my own time: Gone Would I recommend it? No Will I still play? Probably not and that s the problem

They also don't seem to understand community feedback and often implement systems that make problems worse or create whole new problems. Toxicity is no stranger to PVP but it seems to have festered particularly in DBD. My speculation would be the Asymmetric aspect to the game pits Killers vs Survivors- a fun win on one side can often be a toxic loss on the other. The game has unfortunately stopped being fun for me by itself. I only really play it with friends or my wife. I have noticed a trend of: the fun of playing the game diminishes the longer you play, but it often requires friends to play. So someone gets you into the game, quits playing; so you find someone else to play with, and quit playing yourself; and the cycle continues. Review Counter-Strike has been the gold standard of competitive shooters for over two decades, and with Counter-Strike 2, Valve set out to modernize the experience without losing what made the franchise so addictive in the first place. The result is a game that feels familiar in its bones but noticeably sharper, smoother, and more polished on the surface. Gameplay The core loop hasn't changed: two teams of five, one side planting a bomb, the other defending the site, rounds won through tactics, aim, and economy management. If you've played CS:GO, you'll feel at home within minutes. What's different is how everything responds. Movement feels tighter, peeking corners is more readable, and smoke grenades are now fully volumetric they react to gunfire, bullets punch temporary holes through them, and they interact with the environment in ways that add a real layer of strategy to executes and retakes. Gunplay still rewards precision and discipline over spray-and-pray instincts. Recoil patterns are familiar enough for veterans to adapt quickly, while new players have an easier time reading what's happening on screen thanks to clearer visual feedback. Graphics and Performance Built on Source 2, the game looks like a genuine generational leap from its predecessor. I like this game, and I really want to love it, but several major design flaws are pushing me away. The Grind: If you see a video of a content creator running a sick build on The Trapper and want to try it as a new player, you are in for an awful time. The general perk pool is limited, meaning you have to unlock other characters' teachable perks. Here is the issue tho, many top tier perks belong to licensed killers, forcing you to spend real world money just to access them. Even for non licensed characters, Iridescent Shard gain is painfully slow averaging roughly 300 Shards per player level up, which requires several matches of playtime. Meanwhile, the Shrine of Secrets is still heavily outdated. After all these years, it still only offers two random killer perks and two random survivor perks a week. 90 of the time, the selection features terrible or niche perks you ll never actually want. The Balancing A lot of survivor perks are genuinely unhealthy and designed to make killing a singular survivor the hardest part of the round (which is worse since hooking multiple survivors without a certain build is not optimal). Perks like Should the Burden or Decisive Strike (called will to live now) act as massive safety nets that prevent killers from securing pressure, and they are highly abusable by coordinated teams. Meanwhile, perks like Vigil allow survivors to recover from Exhaustion status effects 60 faster mid-chase, giving them access to perks like sprint burst and lithe way sooner. If you are playing a low tier killer with zero mobility, chasing these survivors is the most miserable experience imaginable. That said, I m not a whiny killer main, the killer side has massive balance issues too. Killers like The Nurse completely bypass the core mechanics of the game (pallets and windows), which remains incredibly unhealthy. High tier killers stacking four regression perks make the game a grueling, slow motion chore for survivors, same with slugging builds. The root problem is that Behaviour often balances the game around the uncoordinated Solo-Queue experience rather than competent, high level lobbies. Too many mechanics are designed to help players erase massive positional mistakes by just pressing one button to get the value of a lifetime. The Survivor Side The more you play, the more you realize that survivors are nothing but a catalog of glorified cosmetic skins. Unlike killers, who have completely unique powers, every survivor plays exactly the same. Once you unlock a survivor's three unique perks to be usable by everyone else, that character has zero gameplay identity. Spending real money or grinding thousands of Shards for a new survivor feels unrewarding because you are essentially just buying a new character model. Unless you just love the character's aesthetic, survivors aren't worth buying beyond their perks. The Positives Both killer and survivor are genuinely a blast to play if you don't take the game too seriously. The unique chase music for different killers are phenomenal. Even if some killer powers borrow mechanical elements from older ones, learning the micro mechanics of a new killer's power keeps the gameplay fresh. The developers consistently support the game with events, Tome lore, and major licensed horror icons that keep the community engaged. Final Thoughts: There is a fantastic game buried beneath a mountain of issues. However, the game suffers from a bad reputation because each patch has a tradition of spawning game breaking bugs, and the balancing remains heavily flawed even after 10 years of its launch. I want this game to succeed, but the developers need to rethink how they handle high level balance and the new player experience. TL;DR: Severe balance flaws, an outdated grinding system, and mechanical asymmetry make the gameplay stale for competitive players. Don't buy unless you plan to play strictly casually for the foreseeable future.

Counter-Strike 2 is what happens when a legendary competitive shooter gets abandoned in a dark alley and left to rot. What should be a game about skill, teamwork, and mechanical mastery has become a circus of cheaters, questionable matchmaking, and developer indifference. The cheating problem is beyond embarrassing. It's not even the fact that cheaters exist every competitive game has them. It's that so many of them are so unbelievably bad at hiding it that you start wondering whether anyone is actually monitoring the game at all. You'll watch people perfectly pre-aim every angle, track players through walls, and make "lucky" plays that would require divine intervention to pull off consistently. At some point you stop asking whether someone is cheating and start asking whether anyone in the lobby isn't. Then there's FACEIT, supposedly the premium competitive experience. In reality, it's like moving from one dumpster fire to another dumpster fire with a slightly different logo. The platform loves advertising competitive integrity, yet somehow manages to deliver some of the most miserable matches imaginable. Reports feel pointless, moderation feels invisible, and the overall experience often leaves you wondering why you bothered queueing in the first place. The developers appear to have mastered the art of doing nothing while pretending they're doing something. Community complaints pile up for months, obvious problems remain unresolved, and meaningful communication is practically nonexistent. Every update feels like it was assembled by a team whose primary objective is avoiding eye contact with the player base. The gameplay itself feels increasingly determined by randomness, poor matchmaking, and whatever suspicious creature happens to be on the enemy team that day. You can spend thousands of hours improving your aim, positioning, and game sense only to lose to someone who looks like they installed the game yesterday and accidentally downloaded a gaming chair enhancement package along the way. I would not recommend this game to anyone seeking a serious competitive experience. The only people I can recommend it to are children whose lifelong dream is to witness the greatest RNG experiment ever conducted on modern gaming infrastructure. Counter-Strike used to be a benchmark for competitive shooters. Counter-Strike 2 feels like a case study in how far a franchise can coast on its reputation before people finally admit the emperor has no clothes. 0 10. I'd have had more fun arguing with a wall.

For many years, I never thought I'd be much of a fan of Dead by Daylight. I've never been much of a horror game fan and have always been more of an MMO RPG and FPS enjoyer. This year, my friends asked me to play the game with them since I had it available through my Steam family sharing library. We played a few games, and those few games quickly turned into many. I ended up enjoying the game so much that I now feel somewhat addicted to it, and I've since purchased the game for myself along with multiple DLCs and in-game cosmetics. The gameplay is incredibly fun and exciting, especially when playing with friends and teaming up against the killers. It doesn't feel overwhelmingly scary like many horror games tend to be, but the thrill of being chased by the killer, or sneaking around not knowing when they're going to appear, still gives you a rush. I also love the fact that there are tons of different abilities (perks) that let you customize how you want to play. You can create builds that allow you to face killers head-on, or focus on stealth and completing objectives as quickly as possible while avoiding chases altogether. As for playing as the killer, I unfortunately can't say too much since I haven't spent nearly as much time in that role. I've mostly enjoyed the game from the survivor perspective. However, from the little time I have spent playing killer, I can say that instead of giving you the rush of feeling like the prey, it gives you the more intense experience of being the hunter. Tracking down survivors one by one and preventing them from completing their objectives can be stressful, but it never feels forced or unenjoyable. Gameplay Experience The biggest reason I liked CS2 is its tight and realistic gameplay mechanics. Unlike many fast-paced arcade shooters, CS2 requires patience, teamwork, map knowledge, and precision aiming. Every bullet matters, and winning a clutch round feels extremely satisfying. The movement and shooting mechanics feel smooth and polished. Learning recoil patterns, utility usage, and positioning made the game more interesting over time. Even after many matches, the gameplay never felt repetitive because every opponent plays differently. Graphics and Visual Improvements Compared to older Counter-Strike versions, CS2 looks much better. The upgraded graphics, lighting, smoke effects, and map redesigns make the game feel modern while still keeping the classic Counter-Strike identity. The new smoke grenade physics are one of my favorite additions. Smokes react dynamically with bullets and grenades, which adds more tactical depth during matches. Maps like Dust II, Mirage, and Inferno look cleaner and more detailed than before. Competitive Nature One of the strongest aspects of CS2 is its competitive environment. Winning matches depends heavily on communication and teamwork. I liked how every player has an important role, whether entry fragging, supporting teammates, or clutching rounds. The ranking system motivates players to improve constantly. Losing can feel frustrating sometimes, but improving aim and strategy over time feels very rewarding. This competitive pressure is what keeps the game exciting. Weapons and Sound Design The weapon mechanics are excellent. Guns like the AK-47, AWP, and M4A1-S feel powerful and satisfying to use. Headshots are extremely rewarding, especially because the game has a high skill ceiling. The sound design is also impressive. Footsteps, reload sounds, grenade throws, and gunshots help players gather information and react strategically. Good audio awareness can completely change the outcome of a round. Multiplayer and Team Experience I enjoyed CS2 even more when playing with friends. Coordinating strategies, making callouts, and celebrating wins together created memorable moments. The teamwork aspect makes the game socially engaging and fun. However, solo queue can sometimes be frustrating because toxic players and poor communication occasionally ruin the experience. Despite this, good matches easily outweigh the bad ones. Challenges and Frustrations Although I liked the game a lot, CS2 is not perfect. Beginners may struggle because the learning curve is very steep. New players often face experienced opponents, which can feel difficult initially. There are also occasional issues with hackers, matchmaking balance, and server performance. These problems can negatively affect gameplay, especially in competitive matches. Still, the core gameplay is so strong that these issues did not stop me from enjoying the game overall. Overall Opinion Overall, I liked CS2 a lot because it combines: Competitive gameplay Tactical teamwork High skill expression Smooth shooting mechanics Strong replay value

What I enjoy most about the game is the tension. Few multiplayer games can create the same feeling of panic as hearing the killer getting closer while you're trying to finish a generator or rescue a teammate. The chase mechanics are easily one of the strongest parts of the game, and successfully outplaying a killer or catching survivors after a long pursuit is incredibly satisfying. The variety of killers and survivors also helps keep things interesting. Every killer brings a different challenge, and learning how to play against their unique powers adds a lot of depth to the gameplay. On the survivor side, experimenting with different perk combinations and strategies gives players plenty of ways to customize their playstyle. There's always something new to learn, which helps prevent the game from becoming repetitive. One of Dead by Daylight's biggest strengths is its incredible line up of licensed characters. The game has become a home for some of the most iconic horror franchises ever created, and seeing so many legendary horror characters in one place is something that horror fans can really appreciate. The original killers are also well-designed and fit naturally alongside the licensed content. The developers have done a great job supporting the game over the years. Regular updates, new chapters, events, and quality-of-life improvements help keep the experience feeling active. It's clear that a lot of effort goes into keeping the game fresh for both new and returning players. That said, the game definitely has its flaws. Balance can sometimes feel inconsistent, and there are moments when certain perks, killers, or survivor strategies can be frustrating to deal with. Matchmaking can also be hit-or-miss, occasionally leading to games that don't feel particularly balanced. For new players, the amount of perks, mechanics, and character abilities can be overwhelming at first. The community can be another downside at times. Like many competitive multiplayer games, you'll occasionally run into toxic players who can make matches less enjoyable. Fortunately, those experiences don't outweigh the fun that the game offers overall. Despite its issues, Dead by Daylight remains one of the most unique multiplayer experiences available. The combination of horror, strategy, teamwork, and intense chases creates moments that few other games can replicate. Whether you're playing with friends or queuing solo, the game consistently delivers memorable matches and plenty of adrenaline-filled moments. Overall, Dead by Daylight is a game that has earned its place as the king of asymmetrical horror multiplayer games. It isn't perfect, but its unique gameplay, strong atmosphere, and constant stream of new content make it easy to recommend to anyone looking for something different from the usual competitive multiplayer experience.

h1 Foreword h1 I'm going to preface this quick review by stating that I love Dead by Daylight, and have loved this game since I started playing this game back on console in 2018 (when it became a PS Plus title) and loved it so much that I bought every DLC that didn't already come with the PS4 edition. That being said, there have been an outstanding number of issues that have plagued this game for the entire 10 years of release - some old issues that were fixed while new issues that would arise as the game furthered in development. h1 The Review h1 First and foremost, Dead by Daylight is b NOT b a game that offers a reliable new player experience. The tutorial has seen some changes over the years and only manages to explain the core mechanics of the game in a vacuum. It is a barebones experience. The game itself can be fun once you can wrap your head around the overwhelming amount of perks, perk combinations, maps and map tiles, and the Killers as well as their unique powers. There is so much to this game that it is impossible for someone to learn precisely how to play this game in an efficient and fun manner without needing to rely on guides or feedback from other players (and I will get to the "other players" part.) The game is riddled with bugs, and with every bug that gets squashed - if it doesn't already take multiple years to do so - there's a new one that pops up. Some bugs have never been fixed (looking at you, Twins and Knight) and are usually the result of a game engine that was recently updated but still manages to break more things than it fixed. Balancing for the game, which is quoted by Behavior Interactive "a fun party game you can play with your friends," is completely thrown out the window in favor of... you know I don't even know i what i BHVR's thought process is behind the lack of proper balancing, really. The matchmaking system, or "MMR system" this game has is fundamentally broken, giving you arbitrary, invisible points based off of individual escapes as a Survivor player and 3 kills as a Killer, while taking i away i those points should you be sacrificed to the Entity as a Survivor or you kill less than 3 people as a Killer. Most games after your initial 10-20 games as a fresh account, you b will b be placed against players around your skill level but the more you play the game, the less consistent this will become. I, as someone with over 1,000 hours now on PC alone with a healthy amount of those hours being split between both roles, have been placed against people of vastly different skill levels in every game I play. This also brings me to the b community. b Now, while this does not apply to every single player in the game and there are some amazing members of said community, it cannot be ignored that this game's community is u toxic. u I am talking the same levels of toxicity that have plagued games like League of Legends and Rainbow 6: Siege. It is a community that is riddled with people who have an "Us vs. Them" mentality, who barely understand the core fundamentals of the game (to no real fault of their own,) where they consistently bicker and moan about game mechanics that are used as they're intended to be. As a Killer player, you're very likely to go against survivors who will leave the game because you hooked them, or throw out the most insane, asinine insults because you slugged them for 60 seconds in a match they were going to lose anyway. As a Survivor player, you'll have Killers who will dominate you and your team, and proceed to "WS" (basically pressing forward then back, repeatedly) on your downed body and refuse to hook you because you blinded them once with a flashlight. Those players are also - usually - extremely toxic in the endgame chat. The community is by far the worst aspect of this game and it's painful for me to even write this because I also love a lot of members of the community who are content creators that try their best to foster a healthier, more nuanced approach to the game. If you're someone who is brand new to Dead by Daylight, reads this review and you still want to buy and play the game then I urge you to proceed with caution and have the understanding that you will not pick up this game and "get it" in just a few hours, nor a few hundred hours. I highly recommend looking up outside sources to learning the game while you're taking the time to play it, as it will help you immensely in beginning to understand the complexity of this game. I recommend playing with friends (if you choose to play Survivor more than Killer) who already have a good amount of experience with the game and if you don't have those, peeking into the Dead by Daylight Discord or finding a community that you can play with because that also helps to enjoy the game more. If you're someone who intends on playing Killer more than Survivor, I cannot stress enough how important it is to be patient and take the time to look up guides on the Killer you want to play the most. Killers are the most unique thing about this game and every single one of them has pros and cons to them. I won't get into the whole tier-list thing that you'll inevitably run into because that's a whole can of worms by itself, but just know that some killers are fundamentally stronger than others by nature of their kits, but that doesn't mean you can't have fun with the weaker ones either. Your experience with the game is going to depend on a lot of factors, so much so that I can't write out all of them in order to properly explain how the game will speak to you. This is all to say that at the end of the day, I cannot in good faith recommend this game to a brand new player who is interested in getting into this game. There are better games out there, with healthier communities that you can be part of if you're looking for that sort of thing. If you're still intending on buying and playing Dead by Daylight, then by all means do so. The game at it's core can be a fun experience and the learning aspect of the game is always what kept me coming back to keep playing. It's an extremely unique game in a market that's oversaturated by the same boring genres, I honestly just wish that BHVR did a better job at both communicating with it's community as well as properly listening to that community when the voices that need to be heard the most are desperately trying to communicate the major issues the game has.

Several key factors contribute to its popularity and enjoyment among players 1. Asymmetrical Gameplay : The game's framework involves one player assuming the role of the killer, while four others act as survivors. This asymmetrical format facilitates a unique balance of power dynamics, requiring survivors to employ stealth, teamwork, and strategy to elude the killer, who possesses enhanced abilities and heightened awareness. Each match presents a different scenario, compelling players to adapt their tactics based on the specific characters chosen, thereby fostering an ever-evolving gameplay experience. 2. High Tension and Adrenaline : The game effectively generates an atmosphere of suspense and excitement. Survivors engage in activities such as repairing generators and healing their teammates, all while remaining vigilant for any signs of the killer. The omnipresent threat creates an adrenaline-laden environment, where a moment of distraction can lead to capture. This constant uncertainty and fear of the unknown serve to sustain player engagement throughout each match. 3. Variety of Characters : "Dead by Daylight" features an eclectic array of characters, encompassing both survivors and killers, each endowed with unique abilities, strengths, and weaknesses. The killers range from fantastical entities to human adversaries, each possessing distinct powers that can significantly influence gameplay. Conversely, survivors possess access to a variety of perks designed to assist in their evasion and survival efforts. This diversity encourages players to explore various playstyles and to experiment with character combinations, ultimately allowing them to identify a preferred approach. 4. Strategic Elements : Effective gameplay hinges on strategic planning and collaborative efforts. Survivors must coordinate their actions to fulfill objectives, such as generator repairs, while making critical decisions regarding healing and concealment. This necessity for communication, whether through in-game voice chat or non-verbal cues, enhances the collaborative aspect of the game. On the opposite side, killers must implement strategic tactics, including psychological manipulation and map awareness, to predict survivor movements while deploying their powers effectively. This interaction of strategies contributes to the game's depth and complexity. 5. Customization and Progression : The game offers extensive opportunities for character customization, allowing players to tailor their survivors and killers with various perks, outfits, and offerings. Progression is rewarded through the unlocking of additional abilities and items, which serve to enhance gameplay. This system not only acknowledges players' efforts but also fosters a sense of accomplishment that makes the pursuit of new content feel worthwhile. 6. Atmospheric Setting : The visual artistry and sound design of "Dead by Daylight" play an integral role in establishing an immersive atmosphere. Each map is designed with distinct, haunting environments that effectively convey a tone of fear and suspense. The sound engineering further amplifies this ambiance; for example, the chilling sounds associated with the killer, such as heartbeats and environmental noises, augment the overall tension and vulnerability that players experience. 7. Community and Events : The game is supported by a robust community and regularly features seasonal events that introduce new characters, cosmetic items, and challenges. These events not only refresh gameplay but also promote a sense of community among players. Engaging with fellow participants, sharing strategies, and participating in discussions contribute to a more enriching overall experience, thereby transforming the game into both a competitive and social activity. In conclusion, "Dead by Daylight" successfully merges strategic gameplay, diverse characters, and a captivating atmosphere, resulting in a highly immersive experience for players. The interplay of teamwork, tactical decision-making, and the thrill of evasion or pursuit creates an engaging cycle of gameplay that retains the interest of both survivors and killers, providing enduring enjoyment.

I have been playing War Thunder since the early days, before it was on Steam, and honestly, the game is plagued with long-standing issues. For a new player, the first few tiers can be genuinely fun. The problems start once you hit certain BRs and begin moving higher in the tech trees. You might expect bigger and more tactical maps as vehicles become more advanced, but the opposite often happens: the higher you go, the smaller and more cramped the maps feel. Many top-tier ground battles end up playing more like Counter-Strike than tank combat, with constant close-quarters fights and very little room for proper positioning. The premium vehicle system feels predatory, especially toward new players. It encourages them to skip the learning process and jump straight to famous vehicles they like, such as the M1A1 Abrams, only to get thrown into high-tier matches where they are completely out of their depth. On top of that, Gaijin has recently been criticized for using AI-generated-looking content for things like skins and profile pictures, which makes the monetization feel even cheaper and more cynical. The worst thing a new player can do is buy a high-tier premium and jump straight into the grind. It is repetitive, unbalanced, and extremely punishing. You will often end up as free food for CAS, helicopters, BMPTs, and experienced players who already understand the game s mechanics. A large part of many teams is made up of people who simply do not know what is happening yet, because the game does a poor job of teaching them and encourage throwing yourself at a high tier. The lack of meaningful game modes is also a huge problem. After all these years, most battles still feel like the same team deathmatch formula. Air battles especially could be so much better with proper objectives and more varied modes, but instead they often feel like chaotic team deathmatch with far too many planes. Ground battles suffer from the same issue. The grind is another major problem. It is slow enough that the game constantly pushes you toward buying premium time and premium vehicles. But once again, if you are a new player buying your way into high tier, you are probably going to get destroyed so you won't get anywhere anytime soon. At this point, the grind speed without premium should honestly be closer to what premium accounts currently get and full premium should just x2 the progress. Ground forces in particular take far too long to progress through, while air grind feels somewhat more reasonable. Vehicle modeling and balance are also frustrating. The director is pro russian and somehow like to do taxe evasion at the same time. If you expect your favorite vehicle to be represented fairly, prepare to be disappointed. Bug reports for NATO and other non-Russian vehicles often seem to require overwhelming documentation with no room for approximation, while Russian vehicles appear to receive more generous interpretation. I do not think approximations are automatically bad, sometimes they are necessary when exact data is unavailable, but the same standard should be applied to every nation. There is also a noticeable pattern where certain mechanics or features are said to be impossible, unsuitable, or reserved for later, only for them to eventually appear in a way that benefits Russian vehicles first. This creates the impression that the game is not applying its own rules consistently. Gaijin has also destroyed a lot of player trust by constantly contradicting its own past statements. They said there would be no modern vehicles then added them. They said there would be no modern premiums then added those too. At this point, many of their promises feel meaningless. And when it comes to approximations in vehicle modeling, this is not some conspiracy invented by players. Gaijin themselves have admitted that they use approximations when exact data is missing. The issue is that this flexibility seems to appear far more often for Russian vehicles, while NATO and other nations are held to a much harsher standard where even strong sources are dismissed for not being perfect. Many other shenanigans I can't fit here. In the end, War Thunder could be massively improved with bigger maps, more varied game modes, proper team-based objectives, fewer players per match, some kind of player rating system with a low bias just to get slightly more balanced games and maybe pair the noobs together, and a more consistent standards for vehicle modeling across every nation, not less Russian bias but a more equal treatment for everyone else. Ah yes, and NO AI.

I played Dead by Daylight back when it first released on Xbox, and honestly, I think part of the magic was that nobody knew what they were doing. Everyone was learning, experimenting, making terrible decisions, and somehow that made the game a lot more fun. I ended up putting a few hundred hours into it because every match felt chaotic and unpredictable. As the years went on, the game became much more optimized. People learned the maps, mastered the mechanics, memorized builds, and naturally things got sweatier. That's around the time I stopped playing. I don't mind losing, but I do miss when everyone was just winging it. One thing Dead by Daylight has always done well is its killers. Most of the killers are memorable and bring something unique to the game. The survivor side has never interested me as much. Outside of cosmetics and perks, they all feel pretty similar, while the killers are where most of the personality and creativity live. Coming back after such a long break was rough. My friends quickly reminded me that I was terrible at survivor. Some matches they would intentionally let me win, and other matches they bullied me so hard I started questioning whether we were even on the same team. Even randoms you'd kill everyone and let me go because of how bad I am at this game. Ironically, I was usually much better at killer. Something about it just clicked naturally for me. Unfortunately, playing killer regularly is also a great way to discover new levels of frustration, so I never stuck with it for long. To the game's credit, it feels like the developers have continued improving it over the years. There are still aspects that feel lacking, but it looks healthier than it did when I left. The main reason I decided to give it another chance? My crush plays it. I want him to chase me. I'm not saying that's a good reason to reinstall Dead by Daylight, but apparently it was enough for me. After hundreds of hours, I've concluded that my issue isn't the game. It's that I have the survival instincts of a boxfish and the situational awareness of a Victorian child wandering into the woods. Overall, Dead by Daylight is one of those games that's at its best when you're laughing with friends, screaming over voice chat, and not taking every match seriously. I still miss the early days, but I can appreciate how much the game has grown since then. I may still be terrible at survivor, though. Normally will not Recommend but I see them trying that is what matters the most.

Racial slurs were thrown at me nonstop, and players openly told me that people like me weren't wanted there. It wasn't the occasional trash talk you'd expect from a competitive game it was relentless, personal, and completely over the top. Every attempt to progress was crushed almost instantly. Groups of heavily armed players hunted me down repeatedly, destroying everything I tried to build before I could even get established. After hours of struggling just to survive, I ended up being captured by a large clan that decided I was more useful as entertainment than as another player. They trapped me, stripped me of everything I'd gathered, and forced me into hours of humiliating in-game labor while mocking and harassing me over voice chat. Every attempt to escape ended with another beating, another cage, and another round of insults. The experience felt less like playing a video game and more like being thrown into a lawless wasteland where the most aggressive and cruel people were rewarded for making everyone else's experience miserable. What should have been an exciting survival adventure turned into an endless cycle of harassment, intimidation, and frustration. By the time I finally logged off, I wasn't angry anymore I was exhausted. Rust didn't just waste my money; it consumed hours of my time and left me with one of the most miserable multiplayer experiences I've ever had. CS2 right now isn t a game, it s a psychological experiment Valve is running to find out how long the human nervous system can last before voluntarily switching to farming in Minecraft. It s like a competitive FPS and an anxiety attack simulator had a child. It s full of cheaters, so sometimes the real question isn t whether you re playing well, but whether the enemy can see through walls or is just having a good day. Half the matches already feel suspicious enough that instead of a killcam, you could film a documentary called How NOT to cheat in an obvious way. Matchmaking: Matchmaking is its own universe. With 5k ELO, you can easily get thrown in with 9 10k players. It s like riding a bicycle against Formula 1 drivers, while the system pats you on the back saying, this will be good practice for you. The ELO system also has a special reward: if you leave a match because it s literally unplayable, you get a nice big penalty, as if you were the problem not the fact that you re currently in a troll festival or cheater simulator. Death behind the wall DLC : New CS2 feature: Are you behind cover? You die. The hit registration and subtick system sometimes seem to have a life of their own. You see the headshot, you feel it, you re already about to celebrate, and then the game says no. The enemy turns around and takes you out with a single shot. Teammates: Team spirit sometimes is like a fragile IKEA piece of furniture: in theory it holds together, in practice it falls apart after the first round. The best combination: someone who teamkills trolls flames all at once. That s a full event. Teamkilling is one of the most honest moments in the game. There are times when you get accidentally headshotted in spawn, and your teammate just writes in chat: mb ... Voice chat sometimes feels like a mix between a family argument, a rap battle, and a panic attack: REPORT HIM STFU YOU BOT I AM CARRYING while someone is breathing into the mic like Darth Vader. The best part is when someone tries to find out who s to blame after every round. If you win: they carried. If you lose: everyone else is a bot. If it s a draw: somehow you re still the problem. And of course there is always that one guy who is AFK, but occasionally comes back just to ask eco? before disappearing again, as if he just checked in to see if you re still suffering. The most brutal part is that every match has one common element: five strangers, all completely convinced that it s the other four who are losing the game.

I really wanted to enjoy this game, but after spending a lot of time with it, I can honestly say it has been one of the most frustrating gaming experiences I have had. The game has potential, and that is probably the worst part, because you can clearly see that it could be something much better. Instead, it feels abandoned, unfinished, poorly managed, and focused more on taking money from players than actually improving the experience. One of the biggest problems is the FPS and performance bugs. The game runs terribly far too often, even on systems that should be able to handle it. Random frame drops, stuttering, freezing, lag spikes, and unstable performance make the game feel broken. It is extremely annoying to lose fights or fail objectives not because of skill, but because the game suddenly decides to drop frames or freeze at the worst possible moment. Performance problems have existed for a long time, and yet they still feel like they have not been properly fixed. Another major issue is that the developers do not seem to care enough about the actual problems players are reporting. Updates either take too long, ignore the biggest issues, or focus on things that do not really improve the core gameplay. Players have been asking for basic fixes for years, but many of the same problems are still there. It gives the impression that feedback is being ignored unless it is related to something that can make the game more money. The lack of a proper anti-cheat system is also unacceptable. Cheaters ruin matches, destroy the competitive experience, and make honest players feel like they are wasting their time. A game like this needs strong anti-cheat protection, but instead, it feels like cheating is not taken seriously enough. When players constantly run into suspicious behavior and nothing meaningful happens, it makes the whole game feel unfair and pointless. Player support is another huge disappointment. When something goes wrong, it feels like there is nobody there to actually help. Reports, complaints, and support requests often feel ignored or handled with generic responses. Good player support is important, especially in a game with so many bugs and issues, but this game makes players feel like they are on their own. If the developers want people to keep playing, they need to treat the community with more respect. The maps are also a serious problem. Some maps still feel unfinished even after many years. There are areas that look incomplete, poorly designed, unbalanced, or simply neglected. After this much time, there is no excuse for maps to still feel like early-access content. Players should not have to wait year after year for basic improvements that should have been completed a long time ago. Worst of all, the game gives the impression that it only cares about money. Instead of fixing FPS bugs, adding proper anti-cheat, improving support, finishing maps, and listening to players, the focus often seems to be on selling more paid content, cosmetics, passes, or other monetized features. It feels like the game is treated more like a cash machine than a project that the developers truly care about improving. Overall, this game is disappointing because it could have been great, but it is held back by poor performance, lack of anti-cheat, weak player support, unfinished maps, and developers who seem more interested in money than fixing the actual game. I cannot recommend it in its current state. Until the serious problems are fixed and the developers start listening to the community, this game deserves criticism.

Counter-Strike 2 (CS2) stands as the successor to one of the most iconic tactical shooters in gaming history. By transitioning from the aging CS:GO engine to Source 2, Valve aimed to modernize the experience while preserving the core competitive integrity that defined the series for over two decades. --- The Good: Refined Mechanics and Competitive Depth Source 2 Engine: The visual overhaul is significant. Lighting, textures, and particle effects are drastically improved, making the game look sharper and more immersive. Dynamic Smoke Grenades: This is arguably the most impactful gameplay change. Smokes are now volumetric objects that interact with the environment. They react to bullets and explosions, allowing players to clear lines of sight temporarily a feature that adds an incredible layer of strategic depth. Sub-Tick Architecture: Valve introduced a new "sub-tick" update system intended to bridge the gap between high-tick rate servers and lower-tick environments. While controversial at launch, it fundamentally aims to make movement and shooting more responsive and consistent across all player tiers. The Premier Mode: The revamped matchmaking system offers a clear, ELO-based ranking path that feels more professional and rewarding than the traditional matchmaking ranks. The Fun: The "Culture" of CS Skin Economy: The digital economy surrounding CS2 is unmatched. Collecting, trading, and showcasing skins is a game in itself, often keeping players engaged even when they aren't actively grinding ranks. The Community Custom Servers: From intense "Surf" maps and "KZ" (parkour) servers to casual community modes, the social aspect of jumping into a server with friends remains the heart of the experience. The "Clutch" Moments: There is no adrenaline rush quite like being the last player alive in a 1v3 situation, successfully defusing the bomb, and hearing the roar of your teammates. These high-stakes moments are what make the game legendary. The Bad: Challenges and Frustrations Anti-Cheat Issues: Despite the introduction of "VAC Live," the game continues to struggle with cheaters in higher ranks. Many long-time players feel that the current anti-cheat system is insufficient to handle the evolving complexity of external software. Performance Inconsistency: While the Source 2 engine looks great, it demands more from hardware than its predecessor. Many players with mid-range setups have experienced inconsistent frame rates (stuttering) that can be fatal in a competitive shooter. Content Deficit: Since its release, many legacy maps, community game modes (like "Arms Race" or "Danger Zone" variations), and specific tactical elements from CS:GO have been slow to return or are missing entirely, leading to a sense of "less content" compared to the refined state CS:GO reached before its retirement. --- Final Verdict Counter-Strike 2 is a foundation-level upgrade. It successfully brings the franchise into the modern era with better visuals and smarter utility mechanics. However, it still carries the weight of a transition period. While the core gameplay remains the "gold standard" of tactical shooters, the community is still waiting for Valve to refine the anti-cheat and bring back the depth of content that made the previous iteration feel so complete. --- As you continue to climb the Premier ranks and manage your current loadout, do you feel that the recent balance patches have significantly impacted your personal playstyle or weapon preferences?

It often seems like cheaters can play for long periods without consequences, which makes legitimate players wonder why they should even bother taking matches seriously. CS2 has the foundation of a great game, but right now it's being dragged down by cheaters, trolls, and poor enforcement. Until Valve properly addresses these issues, it's difficult to recommend.

This game would be a lot more fun if it didn't incentivize you to treat it as a full-time job. And the relevant changes to the game mechanics are so simple that they're already common on custom servers. It's really weird to see the contrast between custom servers and the vision the developers apparently have, based on the tumorous experience that is official servers. Because there actually is a lot to like: Scrappy art style and atmosphere, unforgiving combat, and tons of PvE progression routes that don't involve killing every player that moves to steal their stuff. But then each update seems to double down on the idea that you must fight other players to accomplish anything, you must be logged on at all times, and you must not waste your time on a job or studies, meaningful relationships, hobbies, basics like sleep or exercise, or even any other games. You WILL grind out the high-tier monuments to get blueprint scraps, and you WILL construct an armored fortress for your stuff, or you will get stomped by those who did so faster than you. I've been around since the days when zombies were still in the game, and every big update has left me wanting to like the game's many positives, if only it respected my time and sanity. The community is notorious for being toxic, but that shouldn't be a surprise with mechanics like this. How many people are going to reach Tier 3 on a high-population official server and come out okay? Credit to Facepunch for at least supporting custom servers where this nonsense can be mitigated, but I don't understand why they think the vanilla experience would be fun for most people.

Counter-Strike is, without a doubt, the greatest game of all time for me. I've been playing Counter-Strike for over 20 years, and no other game has managed to keep me coming back for so long. Over the years, I've met some amazing people through this game. Some of them became close friends, and a few I even met in real life. Very few games can create connections like that. The gameplay is still fantastic. The movement feels responsive and satisfying, and the hit registration and feedback are usually instant and accurate. It's easy to get into, but incredibly difficult to master, which is one of the reasons why Counter-Strike remains relevant after all these years. The maps are excellent, ranging from timeless classics to the occasional new and exciting community-made maps that keep things fresh. The graphics and the Source 2 engine are also a clear improvement and provide a modern look without sacrificing the core Counter-Strike experience. Would I recommend Counter-Strike 2? Honestly, I would if it weren't for several major issues. The cheating problem remains one of the biggest flaws of the game. Even worse, casual modes such as Deathmatch and Arms Race have become infested with bots to the point where they are practically unplayable at times. The overall selection of casual game modes is also surprisingly limited for a game of this size and age. What makes this especially frustrating is the impression that Valve is either unwilling or unable to meaningfully address the cheating and bot problems. From a player's perspective, there seem to be very few effective measures being taken, while update after update focuses heavily on new skins and cosmetics. What started as an incredible local multiplayer experience during my youth now feels like it's slowly crashing into the ground. Meanwhile, players are expected to get excited about the next case, sticker, or weapon finish. Another thing that has changed for me is the whole case-opening experience. It simply doesn't feel rewarding anymore. What used to be an exciting little bonus has become something I barely care about nowadays. Opening cases no longer gives me the sense of anticipation or satisfaction it once did, making the constant focus on skins and cosmetics feel even more disconnected from the issues that actually affect the gameplay experience. In the end, Counter-Strike 2 is still an amazing game at its core. The foundation is as strong as ever, and I will continue to play it. However, in its current state, I simply cannot recommend it to new players. Great game. Poorly managed problems.

As a player, Counter-Strike has always been an absolute legend in my eyes not just because of its pure, timeless gameplay, but because of the massive, passionate community that has kept it alive for over two decades. CS2 finally brings that legend into the Source 2 era. The visual upgrade is immediate: lighting, textures, and completely rebuilt maps like Overpass look stunning. Volumetric smoke grenades are a genuine game-changer, reshaping tactics in ways that feel fresh and strategic. The sub-tick system was meant to make actions more responsive, but the result is mixed. Shooting often feels crisp, yet movement and spraying can feel inconsistent compared to the old 128-tick servers, leading to frustrating "what you see is not what you get" moments. The weapon loadout adds personalization, but the removal of casual modes stings. Cheating has also migrated seamlessly, and Valve s anti-cheat needs significant work. Despite these issues, the core experience remains as addictive as ever. Premier mode offers structured competitive play with visible ratings. It's free-to-play, gorgeous, and the foundation is strong. CS2 is a brilliant update that still feels incomplete an 8 10 today, with every chance to become a masterpiece once Valve polishes the rough edges. Recommended.

This game is a far cry from what CS:GO was in the past, but CS:GO wasn't perfect either. It had its own problems, like cheaters and bad voice chat moderation, but it also had a better engine (Source 1), faster movement, and better shot registration. If Valve focused on gameplay before skins and cosmetics, it is entirely possible for CS2 to be amazing with just a few adjustments. It's frustrating to spray down a player, run behind a wall, and still die because of the 64-tick (subtick) system it's bull and not fun. Visually, the game looks amazing, and I'm running 200 FPS even with OBS and Firefox open, but they can still do so much better. In CS:GO, movement was indeed way faster, more skillful, and fun to use; here, it feels "noobified," slow, and built for newer players. Of course, new players are what keep a game alive, but this approach backstabs the older fanbase that has been here since 1.6. The only thing I feel they did somewhat right was the empty magazine reload update, since it forces you to remember not to "Call of Duty reload." Other than that, Valve focuses too much on skins, and it feels like everything else is being thrown away or discarded. To be fair, I only started playing a year and a half before writing this review, so I only played a little bit of CS:GO. Still, GO felt much better though not by a massive milestone like some people claim. If they fix the anti-cheat, hit registration, and movement, I think more people will call this their "forever game." I hope Valve fixes these issues and rethinks the future of Counter-Strike altogether. We are not just numbers for your monthly income; we are people, and we should be heard and listened to more often. Without that connection, this game will become just like Overwatch 2: a game past its prime and heading downhill.

DBD Mobile wasn't better because of fancy graphics or licensed IPs. It was better because it was actually fun. I've switched over to Violent District on Roblox for now. The graphics are clear, simple, and don't constantly distract me with random bushes, clutter, and questionable hitboxes. Recently I came back to DBD after about 5-7 months away and played my first matches as both Killer and Survivor. First of all, the FOV is a complete joke. Half the time I can't even tell what I'm looking at. Everything feels cramped, cluttered, and distracting. It's like someone took a monitor with a 1:904044949 aspect ratio and said, "Yeah, play with that." As Survivor, every match felt like I was paired with either infants or lab-grown monkeys being trained in some secret experiment. Nobody does generators, teammates sandbag each other at loops, nobody seems to understand basic pathing, and the Killer is usually running the sweatiest build imaginable. And before anyone says "skill issue," no. The problem isn't that I suddenly forgot how to play. During my break, I played multiple DBD-inspired games and had no problems. The issue is that DBD feels completely different from what my muscle memory expects. As Killer, I decided to play Nurse. Somehow people were landing flashlight saves from angles that looked physically impossible, including what felt like directly behind my head. Four generators popped before I even got meaningful pressure. Then after barely scraping together a 4K at the last second before the final survivor escaped, I got told to kill myself in endgame chat because I won. The funny part? I was running aura-reading perks specifically to help compensate, and they barely provided any value. Nurse feels sluggish, and her blinks honestly feel slower and shorter than I remember, even when fully charged. In my opinion, the developers need to stop polishing their collection of new licensed IPs and catering exclusively to pro-player tryhards. Instead, they should spend some time making the game more accessible for people who genuinely want to learn and improve. In other DBD fangames, I'm a strong looper. I can keep killers occupied for multiple generators and consistently survive chases. Here, I feel completely lost. The visual clutter, pacing, and overall gameplay flow make it hard to understand what's even happening half the time. I don't mind losing. I mind feeling like I'm fighting the game itself. Dont waste money
