h1 Counter this Strike h1 I grew up with Counter-Strike. Back in the days of Counter Strike 1.6 and Condition Zero, this wasn't just a game it was THE game. Everybody was talking about it. If you had a computer, you had Counter Strike, easy as that. Back then, we didn t have automated matchmaking like now. We had to find clan matches through IRC and websites, communicate through TeamSpeak, and spend hours on fixed community servers making actual friends. Whether we were playing a serious clan match at the top of the ladder, or just chilling on surf and aim maps, it was all about the community and having fun. Counter-Strike 2 is a modern evolution of that formula, but for a veteran like me, it s also a stark reminder that you can't truly go back to the good old days. b Where it still strikes: b b Gameplay Adjustments: b Mechanically and visually, Valve has done an incredible job bringing the game into the modern era using the Source 2 engine. The lighting is beautiful, and shadows actually impact gameplay now, allowing you to spot an enemy holding an angle just by looking at their shadow on the wall. The star of the show is the dynamic smoke grenades. The fact that smoke now fills spaces realistically, pushes through broken windows, and can be temporarily cleared or shot through using HE grenades is a smart mechanical addition. It adds a whole new layer of depth without ruining the core formula that made it great. b Get Good: b At its absolute core, Counter-Strike is still one of the most rewarding competitive shooters out there. In a modern world flooded with "hero shooters," ultimate cooldowns, and random wall-run mechanics, CS2 still remains very minimalistic. It is just your aim, your positioning, and your crosshair placement against the enemy. When you get into a proper, quiet 1v1 clutch situation with the bomb ticking, that old adrenaline rush from the 1.6-days is still right there. There are not many competitive games like it, and this is why it's still on top. b Quality of Life Improvements: b Valve completely overhauled the sound design in CS2, making directional audio far more accurate. You can pinpoint exactly where a footstep is coming from. There are also little quality of life upgrades, like being able to sell back weapons you bought by mistake during the buy phase, or seeing a visual radar ping showing exactly how far your footsteps can be heard. This really makes the game feel much more polished. b The Core Gameplay: b Ultimately, the foundation of Counter-Strike still remains mostly untouched. Valve didn't try to reinvent the wheel here because they didn't need to. It's perfect as it is. The loop of buying weapons, managing your team's economy, planting or defusing the bomb, and holding choke points is exactly the same as it was twenty years ago. If you win a round, it s because your strategy worked or your aim was better. It s comforting to see that despite the massive engine upgrade, a classic flash or a headshot still yields the exact same satisfying result as before. b Where it gets countered: b b The Community is Toxic: b The social soul of the game has sadly been completely stripped down. Valve s reliance on automated Premier matchmaking has killed the old community server culture. Playing now is also a toxic lottery. If you solo-queue, you are almost guaranteed to end up with a teammate who uses a microphone made out of a potato or someone screaming orders and acting like a know-it-all before the first pistol round is even over. Everyone acts like they are playing for an Esports team, and that's pretty annoying. b The Hitbox: b The game fails to feel as crisp as the older versions. There are still frustrating moments where hitboxes feel off. Having a clean headshot seemingly vanish into thin air because the sub-tick system had a minor existential crisis is incredibly frustrating. My aim wasn t perfect back in CZ, but at least when I clicked on a head, it stayed clicked. The netcode somehow feels worse here. b Virtual Casino: b CS2 has a severe identity crisis. It sometimes feels more like a gambling simulator for teenagers than an actual shooter. The entire culture has shifted toward virtual weapon skins, knife values, and opening weapon cases. It is sad to watch teammates get instantly killed mid-round because they are too busy spamming the inspect key to look at their really expensive digital knife instead of holding an angle. Ever since games like Overwatch and Valorant started this massive shift where skins are all that matter, it's just been ridiculous. Now weapon skins and knives can cost more than a month's salary. The microtransactions have just gone completely crazy, and it's really sad to see the terrible direction the gaming world is going towards. b The Anti-Cheat Problem: b Valve s VAC (Valve Anti-Cheat) system is in a terrible state, particularly in high-tier Premier matches. Spin-bots, wall-hacks, and aim-bots are everywhere, forcing the serious community to abandon Valve s official servers entirely to play on third-party platforms like FACEIT just to get a fair match. On top of that, Valve completely deleted CS:GO from Steam to force everyone onto CS2, erasing over a decade of community history, achievements, and custom maps, while launching CS2 with significantly less content than the game it replaced. That was a stupid decision in my opinion. b The Sweat isn't Worth It: b CS2 is simply no longer designed for casual enjoyment. It demands your entire life. The "meta" is so hyper-optimized that if you can't treat the game like a second job, you are just fodder for people who spend 8 hours a day grinding Premier mode. It offers very little joy for the returning veteran who just wants to log on for an hour or two a week to relax. Trying to play this casually is just not fun. b The final verdict: b It breaks my heart to give this a thumbs down because Counter-Strike shaped my youth as a gamer, and Valve has technically built a highly impressive sequel here. But while the game looks better than ever, the awesome community culture has been replaced by a toxic, competitive machine that is flooded with cheaters and requires too much of your life to enjoy. If you are a veteran looking to relive the glory days of IRC, TeamSpeak, and local clans, save yourself the heartbreak. It s a great Esport to watch, but the magic of the good old days is gone.

0 10 The Cheaters Have Better Matchmaking Than Players Counter-Strike 2 feels less like a competitive shooter and more like a social experiment designed to test how much suffering a player can endure before uninstalling. The anti-cheat situation is so bad that every match feels like a coin flip between playing Counter-Strike and starring in a live demonstration of "How Walls Work." Trust Factor? Nobody knows what it does anymore. Good players get punished, questionable players get rewarded, and everyone gets thrown into the same digital dumpster fire. Then there are the servers. Nothing says "premier competitive experience" quite like dying three business days after reaching cover. Every gunfight feels like you're arguing with the server about what actually happened. Bugs survive longer than most esports careers. As for Gabe Newell, at this point I picture him as a giant greedy fox sitting on a mountain of case keys, occasionally peeking down at the player base and saying, "Have you considered opening another crate instead of fixing the game?" CS2 somehow took one of the greatest competitive games ever made and turned it into a trust-factor lottery running on servers powered by wishful thinking. Recommended? Only if your hobbies include packet loss, existential despair, and trying to determine whether your opponent has incredible game sense or just a second monitor showing the entire map.

For users who value long-term asset security, infrastructure stability, and progress, this game is a net-negative operational environment. Counter-Strike 2 is truly a masterpiece of modern gaming. There s honestly nothing more satisfying than loading into Premier, winning a few rounds, and then getting instantly headshotted through three walls by a level 2 account named xXPutinLover69Xx. The adrenaline rush of losing 400 ELO to someone spinning at Mach 5 while VAC quietly observes in spiritual silence is an experience no other game can replicate. Speaking of VAC wow. What an incredible anti-cheat system. I especially appreciate how it gives cheaters enough time to fully explore their creativity before considering any action. Why ban them immediately when they can ruin hundreds of matches first? Truly player-first design philosophy. One of my favorite aspects of CS2 is the cultural enrichment. Before playing, my Russian vocabulary was limited to vodka. Now, thanks to my incredibly friendly teammates, I can confidently recognize phrases like Cyka Blyat, idi nahui, and several other beautiful expressions screamed directly into my ears at 140 decibels after losing pistol round. It s basically free language lessons. The matchmaking experience is also second to none. Every game feels like a social experiment. Will your teammates communicate? Will they buy rifles? Will they understand what a bombsite is? Nobody knows. Sometimes I get paired with tactical masterminds who rush mid with a Nova every single round while blasting music through their microphone. The unpredictability keeps the game fresh. And let s not forget the community. Nothing builds character faster than being told to uninstall by someone who finished the game 4-19 while permanently flashbanging the team. The emotional growth I ve experienced from these interactions has been invaluable. Performance-wise, CS2 runs amazingly too. I especially enjoy how every update introduces exciting new FPS drops and mysterious stutters. It s like opening a loot box, except the reward is input lag. Overall, Counter-Strike 2 is more than just a game. It s a test of patience, sanity, and emotional stability. Whether you re losing ELO to blatant cheaters, learning Russian profanity from your teammates, or questioning your life choices after queueing just one more game at 2AM, CS2 always delivers a memorable experience. 10 10 would get wallbanged by a fresh account again.

So. I personally play on Xbox more than PC (as evident by hours, I bought it for PTB purposes). I have around 1k hours on this game in total, and as far as if I would recommend it to other people? It's... complicated. I think the gameplay loop is genuinely great, and I think the unique ways matches can turn out with each killer power and perks in theory gives incredible variety and re-playability. Unfortunately, the people who play this game do not want it to be that way, and the people who make the game don't care to invoke more variety into it. The devs aren't incompetent, but their vision and the communities vision seem to differ, and the overwhelming resistance against a health chapter is slowly vice gripping the game to death. Between a toxic community, a mediocre development team that only seems to focus on new killers (not even really maps or survivors), trying to get into this game now is a death wish. You'll be spending the price of around 2-3 new games on DLC to get everything you want, and then spending around 4-500 hours to get all the perks and then MAYBE you'll get to use a handful of them if you want to win and play the game with a CHANCE to get out or to get 3 kills. Right now, the balance and the complete resistance from the devs makes me say that I don't think I would recommend this game to new players. Until the grind gets better or the game itself becomes worth the grind, I would implore you to spend your money and time elsewhere, which is unfortunate, because I love DbD, and I don't want to stop playing, and I think the gameplay itself is really good and allows for self expression in a beautiful way. Right now though, I wouldn't say its worth it unless you've already played and are deep into it, or if you're just that determined to play the game.

Where you shot was where the bullet went and it was incredibly rare to see object placement discrepancies due to ping - and when you did see them, it was far less egregious. The crosshair bounces all over the place making it highly difficult to place follow up shots quickly or manage the recoil pattern as the screen shakes preventing reliable prediction. Follow recoil, don't follow recoil, they're both pretty terrible to play with. Especially against people who have played with it for thousands of hours and are used to it. Some people would call it a skill gap - I would call it making the game harder to play than necessary. Weapon balancing is awful. The m4a1 has a 20 round clip? Counter-Strike 2 is still one of the most fun and competitive FPS games ever made. The gunplay is great, the maps are iconic, and there really isn't another game that scratches the same itch. When you get a good match, it's easy to see why people have been playing Counter-Strike for over 20 years. The biggest problem is the cheating situation. VAC feels like it only works when someone is blatantly rage hacking and making it obvious. Meanwhile, there are plenty of players, including Prime accounts, who try to hide their cheats and make them look legitimate. Anyone who has spent enough time in Premier or Competitive knows exactly what I'm talking about. What's frustrating is that Valve is a billion-dollar company with more than enough resources to improve anti-cheat, yet it often feels like the issue isn't a priority. Legitimate players are left questioning whether someone is just having a good game or quietly using assistance that never gets detected. CS2 is still a great game at its core, but it's sad to see it in its current state. The potential is there, the gameplay is there, but the cheating problem continues to hold it back.

It s a ruthless, raw beat that I mix every single day on the server. b As a music artist, I view games through the lens of rhythm, composition, and dynamics. In many ways, this game operates just like a solid production inside a DAW: Rhythm Tempo (BPM): Every round has its own unique groove. Map movement, utility timings, spray control it s pure rhythm section. If you miss a fraction of a second, you fall out of time and get headshotted. Peeking is a perfectly timed drop. Sound Audio: The new engine brought incredible sonic depth. The way the echo of an AWP shot resonates, the metallic click of a Desert Eagle reload, or the spatial positioning of footsteps this is mastering at the highest level. The sound design serves you a ready-made arrangement to predict the enemy's next move. Aesthetics Visuals: The new Source 2 lighting brings out the ultimate depth in skin colors (especially in dark, bloody, and neon compositions). My inventory on the server is an extension of my style just like the cover art of a music album. b Verdict: b CS2 can be frustrating when you have a bad day on the server, but when everything clicks the teamplay, the aim, the positioning it sounds better than the cleanest mix in the studio. This game has hilarious bell curve in terms of fun and playability. At first, The game sucks. no perks, no characters, no builds, steep learning curve, toxic community, hardcore killers, and baby survivors (yourself included). its a game that genuinely demands a lot of time, patience, and money to fully experience, which is no fun at all. Then the game reaches a rising point, you got some perks and characters unlocked, you can finally make cool or fun builds, you've learned some neat tricks, had some good games, had some bad games, and it looks like everything might get better from here, then you get hit with an update. typically for this game this means the release of a new and fun killer whose ability feels a little broken for about a month or two and so everyone and their collective mom plays only that killer, which makes the game suck for a while again. new perks to adjust to, new tricks to learn, new priorities based on the killer. It kinda sucks, but its fun because it keeps the game challenging and alive for a minute before you are playing solely for the grind again. then you reach a certain plateau, you have a decent amount of perks on both sides, you've seen some events, a few new killers, really mastered a kind of playstyle that works for you, learn to accept the community for what it is, and still have some fun matches. This is the first plateau of fun, it keeps you engaged, keeps giving you new tools and toys, higher highs and lower lows, good memories and broken keyboards. and honestly most people should stop here, its about 200-500 hours in and where the game is still safe from higher forms of masochism and insanity. But if you press on you, you reach a peak. its pretty far in and it feels amazing, you finally have everything unlocked, all combinations of fun are available to you. This is the "true win" peak, you can finally hone-in and specialize in a brand of killers and survivors with cool cosmetics and fun gameplay loops like surprise killer, fast killer, range killer, sneaky killer, or slow burn killer or on the other side friendly survivor, objective survivor, bully survivor, or funny survivor. and it is here that the novelty is at an all time high, the grind for accessibility feels earned and the fruits of that labor allow you the freedom and fun that you dreamed of during the whole experience. then it trails off to another plateau, the novelty is dying, but you feel like your experience and knowledge of the game allows you a "new understanding" of the games objectives and loops. after you've honed in your expertise with certain characters, the game becomes less about winning and more about having your own fun. whether you find it as merciless killer or unstoppable survivor, a casual killer with his own fun goals and objectives or survivor running specific builds to pull off cool techs or keep things interesting. this second plateau is the beginning of the end. maybe its prolonged by an update or kept alive by a fun new event, but inevitably its a sign that you are slowly losing the fun this game has to offer. then it falls off, something happens, it gets old or repetitive, the toxicity from others feels laughable, those who play too seriously seem like they are missing the plot, you've achieved all your goals, you come back when you want or when something new happens, and then you learn to either leave it alone or revisit it if your friends want to play. and if you cant stop, its hell, for a completionist like myself, you feel that burning desire to fully conquer small aspects of the game, achievements, killers you never got the hang of, anything new that shows up, and suddenly the toxicity feels real, its like ants who don't understand the game crawling all over a perfect opportunity for a new dish for you to try, and you want to walk away from it, to be done and forget it all, but something always drags you back, a cool crossover, a new killer, a new event, some cosmetic you like, or just an itch to revisit one of the fun times you had just enjoying the game. then you transcend, its done, come back when you like or whenever something cool happens or just stick around and keep pulling cool tricks on babies, blast some music and play like an idiot, get drunk and rage the night away, uninstall, reinstall, set up a custom game with bots just chase them around until its stops being funny. do i recommend this game? sure, why not? there are certainly worse things. you gottta admit its got some cool licenses, a fun and toxic community, some fun gameplay loops, and its fun to play cool tricks or mind game someone so hard they get jump scared off their ass or rage quit because they think your psychic. But I cant say its worth it, in the end you play with a million cool and new fun toys just to watch them fade away and leave you wanting something different, the toxicity can still sneak up on ya, the devs are up to their of shenanigans, and sometimes it feels like their is a little too much of everything, like the game has gotten so big that you fear it will either be FUBAR next update or the community will abandon it eventually or it'll just die horrifically to something dumb like cheating bots, license mess up, or they just shut it down because they hate you. Tldr; good luck, its fun, but its also really crazy and taxing.

The Source 2 transition brought reworked visuals and physics-based smokes that genuinely move the game forward; the smokes are so pretty now you almost want to get lost in them. The sub-tick system changed how shooting feels, and thanks to it I'm absolutely certain every death of mine is perfectly fair (it's not). Still, the movement and gunplay kept that classic bone structure, so veterans feel right at home immediately. On the anti-cheat side, things are better than before now that VACnet has improved, but you'll still bump into the occasional "suspicious" people in Premier. To be honest, I also learned to check my own crosshair placement before blaming a cheater. Despite all that, the competitive depth, economy management, and team play are still the best in the genre. That said, I genuinely miss CS:GO. There was something about its feel, its cleaner simplicity and that old-school identity, that CS2 hasn't fully recaptured for me. CS:GO was just better in a lot of ways, and a part of me wishes I could go back. It's free, constantly updated, and has a massive community. You can spend hours trash-talking with your friends, what more could you want? It's a game every FPS fan should try. Highly recommend, but consider this a warning so your life doesn't get derailed.

Dead by Daylight is one of those games that can be incredibly fun and frustrating in the very same match. Its core concept is still very strong: four survivors try to repair generators and escape, while a killer controlled by another player hunts them down. The idea is simple, but the amount of decisions, perks, maps, killers, playstyles, and possible situations makes every match feel different. The best part of the game is found in those tense moments: when you are being chased, when you manage to save a teammate at the last second, when you hide your tracks, when the killer barely misses a hit, or when a match that seemed completely lost ends in an escape. As a survivor, the game becomes much more enjoyable once you understand that it is not always about escaping. Sometimes it is about contributing: repairing generators, rescuing teammates, lasting long enough in a chase, buying time, or simply making a memorable play. The game also has a lot of variety in characters and builds. You can play in a more cooperative, stealthy, aggressive, altruistic, or casual way. You do not always need to use the most meta perks to have fun, and that is something I really appreciate. The perk system allows for a lot of experimentation, although it can feel overwhelming if you are coming back after a long break or if you are trying to unlock specific abilities. That being said, the game is far from perfect. The balance can be inconsistent, some matches feel unfair, matchmaking is not always great, and the community can be pretty intense. There are games where the killer dominates too quickly, others where coordinated survivors make the killer feel helpless, and others where you depend too much on random teammates. On top of that, the grind to unlock perks and prestige characters can feel heavy, especially if you want to try many different builds. The monetization is also debatable. There is a lot of unlockable content, skins, licensed characters, and DLCs. You do not need to buy everything to enjoy the game, but it is obvious that the experience becomes more appealing when you have more characters available. Still, with patience, you can unlock several original characters using the in-game currency. Visually and sonically, the game fits its identity very well. It may not feel like pure horror after many hours, because you eventually get used to it, but it still keeps a tense atmosphere. Sound is extremely important: footsteps, breathing, generators, the terror radius, screams, and killer effects all matter. When the game works well, it creates moments that very few asymmetrical multiplayer games can replicate. My biggest recommendation is not to play Dead by Daylight expecting a perfectly balanced or relaxing experience. It is chaotic, competitive, sometimes unfair, but also very addictive and unique. It becomes much more enjoyable if you play with the mindset of learning, trying different builds, and accepting that not every match will go well. In short: Dead by Daylight has many flaws, but its formula is just too entertaining. It can frustrate you, hook you, make you close the game angry, and then make you open it again the next day. If you enjoy asymmetrical multiplayer games, tense chases, and the feeling of slowly improving, it is absolutely worth playing. I recommend it, especially if you play with friends or enjoy experimenting with different playstyles.

This game has officially been around for 10 years and I think I've finally put in enough hours to give it a review. I've been gaming for about 30 years and this is easily one of my favorite games of all-time, especially in the multiplayer space. One of the first online games I fell in love with was Splinter Cell Chaos Theory, specifically the Spies vs Mercs mode. To this day, I haven't played anything with quite the same cat-and-mouse style thrill. While DBD differs in so many ways, that primal thrill is present here. Even with hundreds of hours, I am enthralled by the feeling outsmarting and outmaneuvering another human. I am not particularly good at shooters, so the skill this game allows me to express is often more of wit than pure mechanical skill. The game is also overflowing with content at this point. It is overwhelming, but if you play this game in bits a time, it will all come together. Consider focusing on one killer until you master them or playing with one survivor and their perks until you've got a handle. As a horror fan, the number of legends present is jaw-dropping, and the original creations are all characters I've come to know and love over the years. It's true that this game's community can be a bit much and some players can be toxic. With that being said, none of that comes close to making me not want to engage with this game and continue playing for years. Considering what the developers have just shown off during their 10th anniversary stream, there has truly never been a better time to start this game. I HIGHLY recommend giving Dead by Daylight a real shot.

Especially if you play with friends, it turns into pure chaos in a good way. But there s definitely another side to it. Things are far from perfect. Sometimes the game can feel pretty unfair depending on the killer or perks. Matchmaking is also weird one match feels super easy, and the next one you get completely destroyed without even understanding what happened. Playing solo is a whole different struggle too. You never really know what your teammates are doing someone goes down in the first minute, someone is hiding in a corner and suddenly the match turns into chaos, but not the fun kind. On top of that, there s the usual toxic behavior from some players unnecessary BM, rage quits, people throwing games it can really kill the mood. The technical side isn t great either. You ll run into bugs, weird hitboxes, laggy moments, or sound issues from time to time. There are plenty of moments where you just go how did that even hit me? Updates help, but they don t fix everything. And then there s the grind. It takes time. Unlocking perks, leveling characters, building the setup you actually want especially if you re new, it requires a lot of patience. Plus, there s the whole DLC and cosmetic system, which can feel like a lot to keep up with. Still, I keep coming back. There s just nothing else quite like it. It s frustrating, it can drive you crazy sometimes, but it s also weirdly addictive. If you re okay with getting tilted now and then and you like horror games, you ll probably still enjoy it.

With the launch of Premier Mode, Valve aimed to bring the professional tournament experience directly to the casual and hardcore player alike, reducing the community's reliance on third-party platforms like FACEIT. The Pick Ban Phase Premier Mode introduces a sleek veto system where teams take turns banning maps until a single battleground is left. This forces players to expand their map pool rather than just grinding Mirage or Dust II all day. The CS Rating Leaderboards Instead of the classic hidden Elo ranks (Silver, Gold Nova, Global Elite), Premier utilizes a transparent numerical CS Rating (e.g., 12,500, 21,000) paired with regional and global leaderboards. The Good: You know exactly how many points you stand to win or lose before the match even starts. The Bad: The classic competitive mode still exists but tracks ranks individually per map, which fractured the player base and made traditional ranks feel less prestigious.

I can t write about Rust the same way I wrote about other games. There s no gratitude here, no sense of quiet escape or rebuilding. If anything, Rust did the opposite for me it took what little stability I had and chipped away at it until there wasn t much left. At first, it didn t seem like a problem. Rust felt intense, exciting, and unpredictable. Every session was different. You spawn in with nothing, and from that moment on, it s survival gathering, building, defending, trusting the wrong people, losing everything, and starting again. That loop hooks you fast. And that s exactly where things started going wrong. Rust doesn t really let you pause. Even when you log off, the world keeps going. Your base can be raided, your progress wiped out overnight. That creates this constant pressure to stay connected, to keep checking, to make sure everything you built is still there. I started logging in more often, staying up later, telling myself just one more check or just one more upgrade. It stopped being a game and started feeling like an obligation. Sleep got worse. Routine disappeared. Real-life responsibilities started slipping, but it didn t feel urgent in the moment because in Rust, everything feels urgent all the time. If you don t act now, you lose. That mindset slowly carried over into how I lived day to day, except instead of being productive, I was stuck in a cycle of reacting, not thinking. Then came the spending. Skins, servers, anything tied to the game I kept justifying it. Small amounts at first, easy to ignore. But over time, it added up. And because I was already so invested emotionally and time-wise, it felt harder to stop. Like I had to keep going to make it worth it. That s a dangerous trap, and I fell straight into it. The worst part wasn t even losing things in-game it was how much it affected me outside of it. Frustration carried over. Losing a base after hours of work didn t just stay on the screen; it stayed with me. It made everything else feel worse, heavier, more pointless. At some point, I realized I wasn t enjoying it anymore. I was just stuck in it. Rust didn t give me structure like other games did. It didn t calm me down or help me focus. It fed into stress, into compulsive behavior, into a constant sense of not enough. No matter how much time I put in, it always demanded more. And the cost wasn t just time it was money, energy, and pieces of my life that I should ve been protecting. I m not writing this as a dramatic exaggeration. For some people, Rust might just be a game. But for me, it became something unhealthy. Something that took advantage of where I already wasn t doing well and pushed things further in the wrong direction. If anything, it taught me a hard lesson: not every escape is good for you. Some just pull you deeper into the problems you re trying to avoid. I don t recommend Rust not because it s badly made, but because of what it can become if you re not careful. And I learned that the hard way.

Been playing this for way too long and given it too many chances (more hours than what steam says). It's the 10th anniversary and it feels like almost nothing much has improved. Progression feels unrewarding and caters around the meta too heavily in terms of perk choices, killer picks and maps. Even with 309 perks currently in the game, you probably will only see the same perk types being used by most players. Certain perks can cause matches to become unfun and worst case scenario make you second guess yourself since it can very hard to tell whether someone is cheating or not. Killer designs over the years have gotten increasingly uncreative and poorly designed. You can compare most killers released over the past 3 years to older killers and can tell easily how similar they are. The Animatronic Dredge Huntress. The Slasher Dredge Huntress. It's fine for people to be hyped over Jason being added, but its almost ignored and they end up getting the same killer they already had which almost makes it just a new skin for a killer that exists in DBD. The balancing of the killers is absolutely atrocious. Nurse hasn't been fixed in so long you can't even tell you're playing a match of DBD because the gameplay is non-existent, if the Nurse player understands how the power works of which people tend to overexaggerate how hard it is to learn The Nurse. Then you have the opposite, being The Trapper who is probably the saddest icon for DBD since the devs have given him zero respect and no changes for a very long time(maybe some add on changes but he sucks regardless). Also, some killer designs allow for the most boring experience you could have playing this(Nurse included) and there are too many of them. If you want to play against a killer that is interactive then that is a harsh gamble especially considering how people tend to play them. Maps are also atrociously balanced with certain maps having the killer break uncounterable pallets too many times, to awfully big maps that require more travel time than actual gameplay. This does depend on what killers you pick on each map which is mostly fine, but it is inexcusable with how they have not learned over the years what makes a map at least decent. You can tell with the latest map they added, being too large and confusing to navigate with some other flaws like uncounterable pallets. As for the community, it is pretty hard to find some decent people who won't winge, give up, hold the game hostage, etc. Or even just ruin the match by playing an unfun killer or perks even though they might not be intending to make it unfun. If you look up some history of BHVR's fumblings then you'll understand how much they really care. This is roughly the reason why I'm giving up on this game. You spawn naked on a beach holding a rock, immediately get chased by a man wearing a wolf skull, and somehow that s considered normal progression. The game teaches valuable life lessons: never trust anyone, sleep is temporary, and your base is actually public property after 3AM. At first, Rust looks like a survival game. You gather wood, farm stone, hunt animals But after 20 hours you realize the actual objective is emotionally ruining strangers before they emotionally ruin you first. The community is truly one of a kind. A random player might: give you guns, adopt you into a clan, play guitar outside your base, or spend six straight hours camping your front door because you looked at him wrong near Supermarket. And the craziest part? All of this is considered peak gameplay. Rust also has one of the most advanced sound systems in gaming history. Every noise triggers a different medical condition: footsteps cardiac arrest helicopter panic attack satchel charges immediate spiritual collapse You don t log off Rust. You simply leave your belongings unattended for international thieves. The progression system is beautiful too. You grind for 9 hours to finally craft an AK, then die to a naked man with a bow named tax collector. Balanced. The clan experience is amazing as well. Nothing builds friendship faster than: arguing over sulfur, blaming each other after raids, and hearing WHO LEFT THE DOOR OPEN at 4AM. Solo players are especially respected in the community, which is why the game regularly matches them against 14-man groups sponsored by unemployment. The longer I play this game as a killer, the more I hate the dev team for constantly sugarcoating survivors. Every update seems to add more and more ways for survivors to do generators faster and know exactly what their teammates are doing. When you play as the killer, you have to play 5D chess. You need to manage generators, hooks, perks, and how to use them effectively, while also keeping track of what perks the survivors have, what items they're bringing, and where they might be. I'm terrible as a survivor, but you know what? I don't need to be good. I load into a match, sit on a generator for 90 seconds, and two or three other survivors do the same on different generators. If the killer isn't using a meta build or playing a top-tier character like Nurse, you can simply abuse the fact that the killer can only chase one person at a time, and the escape is basically yours. I like to play sneaky. I like using the worst perks imaginable and getting excited when they work even once. Know the map and pallet spawns? As if that matters. The maps are packed with so many pallets and windows that a new player can run in a random direction with zero planning and still stumble into safety, while experienced players can chain loop after loop with almost no risk. Either way, the killer ends up wasting an absurd amount of time just trying to get a down, if they get one at all. The MMR system isn't working at all. Counter-Strike 2: A Disappointing Update to a Classic Counter-Strike 2 was one of the most anticipated competitive shooters in recent years, promising improved graphics, better technology, and a fresh experience for fans of the franchise. Unfortunately, the game often feels more like an unfinished replacement for Counter-Strike: Global Offensive than a true step forward. One of the biggest criticisms I have of Counter-Strike 2 is that it removed features and content that players had enjoyed for years in CS:GO. At launch, several maps and game modes were missing, making the game feel less complete than its predecessor. Many players expected a significant upgrade, but instead found themselves with fewer options. The game's technical performance has also been a source of frustration. While the new graphics engine can make maps look more detailed, some players experienced lower frame rates and performance issues compared to CS:GO. In a competitive shooter where every millisecond matters, these problems can negatively affect gameplay. Another major complaint is the matchmaking and anti-cheat system. Cheating has remained a concern within the Counter-Strike community, and many players feel that the game's anti-cheat measures have not improved enough. Facing suspected cheaters can make competitive matches feel unfair and discourage long-term play. Counter-Strike 2's new "sub-tick" system was advertised as a revolutionary improvement for responsiveness, but many players reported inconsistent experiences. Instead of feeling like a clear advancement, the system became a topic of debate, with some arguing that gameplay felt less predictable than expected. The game can also be criticized for relying heavily on the formula established by previous Counter-Strike titles. While maintaining a classic style is not inherently bad, Counter-Strike 2 introduces relatively few groundbreaking innovations. For some players, it feels more like a graphics update than a true sequel. Conclusion Counter-Strike 2 succeeds in modernizing the visual presentation of the series, but it falls short of the high expectations surrounding its release. Missing content, performance concerns, ongoing cheating complaints, and a lack of major innovation make the game feel underwhelming. While dedicated fans may still enjoy its competitive gameplay, critics could argue that Counter-Strike 2 is a frustrating example of a sequel that does not do enough to justify replacing the game that came before it.

Premier matchmaking in CS2 is far too often ruined by blatant cheating and abusive communication. When the matches are filled with decent people, the game is still excellent. Counter-Strike at its best is one of the most enjoyable competitive games ever made. But in Premier, I am too often placed in matches with obvious spinbot aimbot behaviour, or with players being severely abusive over voice text chat. When that happens, the match stops being competitive, enjoyable, or even worth playing. The worst part is that the system often makes everyone else feel trapped. A player can receive reports from an entire team in the first few rounds, but the rest of the lobby is still stuck waiting for the match to end unless they want to abandon and risk a cooldown. That creates a miserable experience for legitimate players. VAC and the reporting system currently feel ineffective from the player side. Maybe action is happening behind the scenes, but it does not feel visible, fast, or strong enough to protect the Premier experience. CS2 can still be brilliant when the match quality is good. But right now, Premier is too inconsistent and too often ruined by cheaters and abusive players. For the main competitive mode of Counter-Strike, that is deeply disappointing.

Often times they will deliberately choose a different strategy every video just for fun. I know this description might not sound compelling but I just don't even know where to begin describing why I like this game. Really just being a beginner and trying to survive with a primitive setup is fun on its own. There are old military sites and old supermarkets full of loot, some more contested than others. You can build anywhere at all on these enormous maps and the game is pretty unforgiving, however once you get your base established then things start to stabilize and you're afforded some safety and time to think about expanding. Each time you play you will create a base a little more efficient and a little more safe and you will accomplish more and more. Honestly, CS2 has been one of the most frustrating gaming experiences I ve had in a long time. The game looks nice visually, but almost everything else feels worse. Hit registration is completely inconsistent. There are so many moments where you clearly hit headshots and nothing happens. Sometimes you spray directly into someone and deal almost no damage, while on your screen the shots are perfectly on target. The hitboxes feel broken, especially during peeking. Gunfights often feel random instead of skill-based. Matchmaking is another disaster. Almost every game is unbalanced. You either get brand new players on your team who don t even understand basic utility usage, or you play against obvious smurfs with thousands of hours destroying everyone. There s barely any middle ground, so competitive matches rarely feel fair. Performance is also terrible. FPS drops, stuttering, random freezes, input lag all of this still exists even after multiple updates. Sometimes the game feels smooth, and the next match feels completely different for no reason. Sub-tick was supposed to improve responsiveness, but instead the game often feels delayed and inconsistent. Cheaters are still everywhere, especially in Premier mode. Reporting barely seems to do anything, and legit players are the ones suffering because of it. At this point, CS2 feels more polished visually than mechanically. The core gameplay shooting, movement, matchmaking is simply not reliable enough for a competitive shooter. Right now the game is more annoying than enjoyable.

I have spent 633 hours in this game. I have watched my crosshair tremble over heads I should have hit. I have clutched 1v3s in silence and then immediately thrown the next round by peeking B long like I invented overconfidence. I sit at 8,500 ELO which sounds respectable until you realise it just means I now lose to people who are precisely as mediocre as I am, but faster. Counter-Strike 2 is not a game. It is a mirror you fire bullets into. The gunplay is still the best in the world. Not because it's smooth or forgiving it isn't but because it is honest. Your spray goes wide because you pulled the mouse wrong. You lost the duel because you peaked at the wrong tick. The game never lies to you. That's both its gift and its cruelty. The maps breathe differently than GO. The sound design rewards obsessive listening. The Premier system will make you feel like a genius for six rounds and then remind you, efficiently and without ceremony, that you are not. At 8.5k, the matches are chess with rifles. Everyone knows the setups. Everyone expects the read. Winning becomes less about mechanics and more about thinking one layer deeper than the guy thinking one layer deeper than you. It is exhausting. I queued again immediately. I do not know if this game is good for me. I know I'm not done with it. 633 hours in. Still undefeated in my own head. 8,500 ELO. Every loss was a fluke.

I discovered Dead by Daylight at the end of 2021. It s a very atmospheric game. You can really enjoy it when you re playing in a party with friends on voice chat - in fact, I d even say it s one of the best games to play with friends. You can have an insane amount of fun. Because when you play with randoms, they just do whatever they want on the map and are ready to throw you under the bus at the first opportunity just to escape through the hatch. And then, annoyed at the whole world, you switch to killer and ruthlessly wipe everyone out. At least that s more fun than getting frustrated with inactive teammates. For randoms, it s completely normal to sit a meter away from you, repair a generator, let you hit second hook stage - and still not unhook you! It might actually make sense to add voice chat or some kind of radio mode so players can communicate in-game. Another thing that really annoys me is the killer playstyle: when you re a lowskill killer, all you can do is camp and tunnel. That just ruins the mood for the entire team. Moments like that make me want to delete the game and never come back. But there are also positive moments-like when you get killers who are genuinely fun to play against, who let everyone experience death on the hook, or who are willing to carry you half-dead to the hatch. That really lifts your mood. Overall, I ve got 400 hours in the game. I don t play it consistently, but every year something brings me back. And it s really nice that you don t get disappointed-the game isn t dying. The developers keep updating it, running events, adding new characters, skins, maps, and so on. You can tell they actually care about the game. There s also a cool website now where you can track your match stats. And I especially want to praise the cross-platform support - it s a must-have. Thanks to that, I managed to transfer all my data, characters, skins, and currency to Steam. It s a shame achievements can t be transferred though - you have to grind them again. Oh wait I meant to say, you don t really grind in this game - you actually enjoy it! It s especially great for people who love horror and have watched movies or shows with these characters. Personally, I really connect with Stranger Things, although I don t like the Eleven skins-that s just personal preference. Vecna is implemented really well. His new skin is amazing. Even the voice sounds very similar, despite not being voiced by Jamie Campbell Bower. And when he looks at me in the lobby from a first-person perspective, it makes me smile every time :) However, during the time I ve been playing, the ranking system has gotten worse. Before, you could lose pips for bad performance, your rank would drop, and people who climbed actually had to sweat for it. After matches, you could see your teammates ranks. Now everything is handled by a hidden MMR system. After a match, you only see your teammates character prestige - but in practice, it means absolutely nothing. I d also like to mention the toxic in-game community - it really annoys and upsets me. People are so aggressive and completely kill the vibe. After almost every match, be ready for someone from your team or the killer to get flamed in chat. Even if you carry and win, there ll be that one rat in your party who writes toxic stuff directed at everyone. Or people will just be toxic for no reason. The chat filter won t help - lol. It s honestly awful. So to everyone who plays or plans to play this game: be kinder, enjoy this vibey game, spread positivity - and don t be toxic pieces of crap ;)

h1 Dead by Daylight Review h1 hr hr h2 Introduction h2 Dead by Daylight is Behaviour Interactive's asymmetric survival horror multiplayer and nearly a decade after launch, it is still the undisputed king of its genre. Four survivors scramble to repair generators and escape. One killer hunts them down using supernatural powers and brute force. Simple concept. Infinite depth. What started as a niche indie experiment in 2016 has grown into one of the biggest ongoing live-service games on PC and console and its best days are still being written right now. hr hr h2 Core Gameplay h2 No two matches ever feel the same, and that is genuinely impressive for a game with such a tight ruleset. The tension between repairing generators and staying hidden is perfectly calibrated every second matters The chases are pulse-pounding, with looping, vaulting, and mind-game mechanics that reward skill on both sides The skill check system keeps survivors constantly alert even during the quieter moments Playing killer feels completely different from survivor it is essentially two games sharing one map Totem cleansing, chest hunting, and hook rescues create natural moments of teamwork without voice chat The asymmetry is the magic. A coordinated survivor team that clicks perfectly is one of the most satisfying experiences in multiplayer gaming. An equally matched killer who reads their movements is just as thrilling from the other side. hr hr h2 Atmosphere Maps h2 Dead by Daylight's world The Entity's Realm is genuinely unsettling in a way most horror games fail to achieve. Each realm has its own distinct visual identity, from the industrial rot of MacMillan Estate to the clinical dread of L ry's Memorial Institute Fog, ambient sound, and darkness do more work than most AAA horror titles twice its budget Procedurally generated tile layouts ensure maps never feel identical between sessions The Entity's influence hooks, corrupted terrain, and those massive claw-like structures creates a constant sense of something ancient watching every trial Walking into a match on a dark foggy Coldwind Farm with distant heartbeats growing louder is still one of gaming's best slow-burn dread experiences. hr hr h2 The Roster Killers Survivors h2 This is where Dead by Daylight truly separates itself from every competitor it has inspired. b The killer roster is extraordinary. b Original creations like The Nurse, The Trapper, and The Artist sit alongside licensed legends Michael Myers, Freddy Krueger, Ghostface, Chucky, Vecna, and many more. Each killer plays completely differently from the rest, with unique power kits that demand different strategies and counter-play from survivors. The licensed crossovers are handled with genuine care and respect for the source material. Seeing Michael Myers stalk you through corn fields exactly as he does in Halloween is a legitimately surreal experience. b Survivors matter just as much. b Original survivors have grown into beloved characters with deep lore across comics, tomes, and in-game stories. The survivor pool is now enormous, covering a wide range of personalities and backgrounds. hr hr h2 Perks, Builds Depth h2 Dead by Daylight's perk system is secretly one of the deepest build-crafting systems in any multiplayer game. Every killer and survivor comes with three unique perks that can be unlocked and mixed across the entire roster Build variety is enormous aggressive builds, stealth builds, generator rush strategies, and altruistic team-focused setups all work On the killer side, the difference between a proper perk-synergy build and a random selection is massive and immediately felt Add-ons and offerings add another layer of customization before a trial even begins The meta constantly evolves as Behaviour balances perks and introduces new ones with each chapter Learning the perk ecosystem is a genuinely rewarding long-term investment. The deeper you go, the more satisfying the game becomes. hr hr h2 Lore Tomes h2 Dead by Daylight's lore is criminally underrated and far richer than most players realize. The Tome system releases story chapters revealing the backstories of killers and survivors through beautifully written journal entries, cutscene memories, and in-world artifacts. The Entity itself is a fascinating cosmic horror concept a creature that feeds on hope and despair, pulling beings from across dimensions for millennia of suffering. If you have ever dismissed DbD as a game without story, the Tomes will genuinely surprise you. Characters like The Artist, The Dredge, and Jonah Vasquez carry some of the most compelling horror writing the genre has seen in years. hr hr h2 Problems h2 Dead by Daylight is exceptional, but it earns its complaints too. Balance remains an ongoing challenge certain killers and perk combinations feel overwhelmingly oppressive at lower skill levels Matchmaking can be inconsistent, occasionally placing new players against veterans with thousands of hours The community has a well-documented toxic streak post-game chat is often best left unread entirely Cosmetic pricing for licensed content is steep, and the archive grind feels padded in later tomes Some older maps have tile layouts that heavily favour one side, and reworks have been slow None of these are deal-breakers but they are real, and new players should know what they are walking into. Thick skin helps. hr hr h2 Final Thoughts h2 Dead by Daylight should not still be this good. Nearly a decade in, most live-service games have faded. DbD has grown into something genuinely special a game that keeps evolving its roster, its systems, and its world while never losing sight of the core loop that made it extraordinary in the first place. b If you love horror culture, it is the ultimate fan experience your favourite villains made playable, treated with real creative respect. b b If you love deep multiplayer games, the perk system alone will keep you theorycrafting for years. b Horrifying, tense, occasionally infuriating, deeply rewarding and completely impossible to put down once it gets its hooks in you. That last part is very much intentional. hr hr h2 Rating h2 9.2 10 One of the greatest live-service games ever made. Horror licensed content done right, endlessly deep build-crafting, and a tension loop that no competitor has managed to replicate after ten years of trying.

One of the hardest games to recommend I've ever played. These hours on my account don't accurately represent the other hundreds of hours I have on other platforms. I've been playing DbD for 6 years, and its the only reason I can even still play, because I've expended considerable effort and watched twenty hours of Otzdarva videos making me semi-decent at best at this game. If you just stumbled onto this on steam and don't know the first thing about DbD, you likely will not enjoy it. If you don't want to watch hours of youtube videos explaining why the killer found you hiding in a corner out of sight, or why you can never seem to catch up to a survivor, you likely will not enjoy it. If you don't have money for or don't want to spend money on characters to gain access to the most basic abilities everyone else is using, you likely will not enjoy it. If you (very reasonably) can't handle the idea of being bad at something for reasons that you can't begin to understand, you likely will not enjoy it. Dead by Daylight is an asymmetrical multiplayer game unlike anything else that ever came before it, because its biggest fight isn't between the hatchet-wielding maniac and his potential victims, it's between the people who have been playing for ten years and the person who saw a video of Springtrap chasing Trevor Belmont and thought it might be fun. There is nothing, and I mean nothing, that this game can or will do to make a new player understand why they won't be good or even passable at the game for many, many hours. You cannot learn the true basics of the game on your own, you WILL have to have someone explain it, and if you want to have a casual experience where you don't care about winning or losing, you are almost guaranteed to be ruining the experience for someone who does, or vice versa. I personally think the game should be free to start. 12 characters sounds like a lot, but once you realize that their perks are passable at best and miles from what you will see 70 of other players using, the game asserts the need to spend either a considerable amount of time, or your hard-earned, honest-to-God dollars to get your hands on the rest of the game. Not just that, but I shudder to imagine how much of the money Behaviour has in their pocket from people who bought this thinking the idea sounded enjoyable, and by the time the refund period was over, they realized it was an unapproachable mess. If you've read all that, and still think you might want to try starting it; if you like watching youtube videos and spending money on characters you don't want to play as; if you want to join the internet's worst abusive relationship, then take my hand, and join the club. The wins are tight, The losses are heartbreaking. The clutches are hype. The moments of just barely getting away from the killer and breaking chase will have you shouting for joy. I'm having fun, but Christ did I have to work for it.

I've got 500-something hours. I play every day usually, it's a huge addiction of mine. If I haven't played for a bit, I start to really miss the game. I love the concept of an eldritch horror keeping people trapped in this cycle of matches trials, and I wish they would make little short videos of the characters interacting at the campfire between matches. I think that would be adorable. Since you play with and against other people, every match is different. Everyone plays a little different and I love the funny moments, the stealth killer jump scares, and I love that I can play with my duo and other friends. It takes real work to get good at this game. It's so rewarding to improve your looping, chasing, etc. skills. I've been playing for over a year and I am finally getting good in chase. But obviously there is always room to improve. I look forward to seeing how my patching changes with experience. A lot of it has to do with learning to think how the other thinks and predicting their decision making split second. I love that. It's so cat and mouse. The cosmetics are great and I love how many characters there are, and the lore. 2v8 is a blast when it's around, I wish they would make it a permanent option, or at the very least let us do custom lobby 2v8 so people can kill bots together. There are some issues, unfortunately. The hit boxes are sometimes really too large or small, and if a killer has bad connection, you might be far ahead of them and it still recognizes it as a hit, not a miss, since on the killer's screen you're within range due to lag. Some maps are horrendous to play, such as midwich or hawkins lab. They should really have done an outdoor map for stranger things. Or perhaps a mall map. Something that isn't so narrow with nowhere to loop. There just aren't enough windows, and once the pallets are gone, there's nothing you can do. And being forced to run down a hallway on either map can be a death sentence if you're against a projectile user. Some of this community is extremely toxic, too. If you're unlucky, you'll get tunneled out and not even play the match. Sometimes survivors are really mean to killers, like they are mad if you 4k or mad if you don't do well in the match, even if you're new to a killer. People are nasty in the comments, so turn them off if you can't handle it. And there's a lot of judgement and stereotypes for playing certain characters that is simply unfounded and uncalled for. I've also encountered people being rude because I am a woman, which is super small minded and silly. It's 2026 people, it shouldn't be a shocker that women, who have the same hands as men do, can play video games. My gender doesn't affect whether I can press buttons in the right order lol. There's quite a bit of 'free' cosmetic content so long as you save up iridescent shards that you earn by simply playing matches. You can also use shards to get some characters. All licenced characters are each about 5 which adds up after a bit, especially on the survivor side if you're trying to get different perks for a build. It sucks to have to pay 5 for a survivor you don't want to play as, because you need one of the three perks they have. It would be great to have an option to buy specific perks on their own, but whatever. I recommend this game if you're a chill person who doesn't get angry with teammates for making mistakes or being purposefully bad sabotaging the match. Or if you like the idea of chasing or being chased and trying to outwit people. Lots of mind games happen in the higher mmr matches. I don't recommend this game to you if you easily get hurt by others or upset by people not doing things the way you wanted. There are going to be bad plays by teammates, whether on accident or on purpose. It's a game. There is no point getting upset over it, especially if it's a genuine mistake that someone made. We've all accidentally dropped a pallet when trying to heal a downed survivor. And sometimes you just have a bad match. If you're the type to tell someone to hurt themselves or uninstall for accidents and mistakes, we do not need you in this community. Be polite, be respectful, and let the game be what it should be: fun! Enjoy your loops, get that cosmetic drip for your main, and may your skill checks be wide and your heals be fast. Have a blast!

I would like to preface this review, with the following: I have not played the game in a substantial amount of time. So it is subject to my opinion of past experiences, still following community updates and having friends active in it. HI! I have a lot of time in this game, not much compared to a larger player base but still have some input. I am not a technical person, I know how to turn my computer on. So this is a review from someone, who simply once played and enjoyed the game. Dead by daylight, is a great game to sink hours into! Its a fun game, to try and run new builds. Experience killer survivor games at a relatively quick matchmaking pace. The graphics, are something I have enjoyed its a visually great game! The soundtrack slaps and the overall vibe of the game is great. However, the community. That is where the problem is with this game. It is a community of people that want to just cause disruption and remove players joy from the game. Running it with friends, can be a great experience and how I would recommend it. Yet, its a game that just eats at your mental and causes frustrations quickly. Solo play, you either are going to having a mediocre game as survivor or have a team that just ignores one another and play a co op game as a single play experience. This it not to say you cant play solo at all, each to their own. As survivor, you can have some really fun games! Games where survivors just want to enjoy it, farm some bp and have a good time. However majority of the games (up to when I played especially) for killers, is built to support "bully squads" don't get me wrong, the goal is to escape. However some players will take this to an extreme, and just torment other players. The matchmaking in this sense felt unbalanced especially if you wanted to learn new killers and or survivors. Since at times you would get matched against sweaty killers who just want to steamroll, and draw the game out (although they have added some stuff to counter this it does not feel effective) The character design, is great some killers survivors are "OP" if used correctly. Lastly, try the game it really is worth it. Go in, and be wary of community. Make some friends where you can and focus there and the game will be worth it more so down the road. My negative opinions are mostly based on community experience rather then the work of the devs themself. So I will still recommend this game, because they deserve that.

After having played this game for a gooooood while I can safely say it's something truly special. I've not put as much gameplay into any game like I have DBD and I think it's because I simply enjoy myself with all aspect of this game. It helps that I'm a tad bit of a perfectionist so there's lots of content for me trying to prestige every character to at least P3! Survivor is extremely fun, especially with friends. Slowly finding the ability to figure out different counters to specific killers and finding unique and fun builds is something wildly entertaining. The only problem I have with survivor is whenever I'm solo queueing and my fellow survivors are extremely confused and lost. Killer is where I've spent the most time on DBD. I have every single killer unlocked and all to P3! I've played them all thoroughly and I love how there's a playstyle out there for literally everyone. You have ranged killers, stealth killers, brute force killers, and even more. And combine these specific killers and their powers with an abundance of perk builds and you've got a time of endless gameplay. Sure there's some days that your killer matches are absolutely draining and you want to scream and throw your computer out the window but otherwise it's great. I hope to see DBD continue to thrive as updates come through! Here's to many many more adventures in the fog!
